msm.intro: A machine service manifest is a written description of an outside service: what it does, where it lives, what it takes and what it gives back. An AI reads the description and calls that service itself. This site keeps the description and never makes the call.

now.title: Right now
now.line: Registering one connects nothing. It publishes a description that an AI can read, and the call is made by whoever read it.

strip.needKeySub: and the key lives on the machine, not here
strip.repeatedNone: no two describe the same thing

list.title: What is registered
list.find: Find by name, address, action, owner or words
list.noMatch: Nothing here matches what you typed.
list.none: Nothing is registered yet. The ready-made ones below are the quickest way to start.

sets.title: The same service, described more than once
sets.lead: {n} of {total} are in a set with at least one other. Two manifests are in a set when they call the same address, or when they offer an action of the same name, and the fact that joined them is on each line.
sets.none: No two of these describe the same thing.
sets.byHostWhy: Every one of them points at that address. They were written separately, and nothing says which is the one to read.
sets.byActionWhy: They call different services and answer to the same action name, so an AI asking for it by name could be handed any of them.
sets.byBothWhy: Joined through a third one: each shares an address or an action name with another in the set.
sets.aloneWhy: Nothing else here calls their address or offers their actions.
sets.aloneOneWhy: Nothing else here calls its address or offers its actions.

ready.title: Ready-made ones that ship with this site
ready.lead: Each is complete: auth, actions, what every action takes and gives back, and a health block. They are the quickest way to see the shape of a good one. Open one, change the address and the fields, and you have written yours.

takes.title: What it takes to use one
takes.key: The key is a name, not a secret
takes.keyWhy: A manifest says which environment variable holds the key, for example DIGITRANSIT_API_KEY. The value lives on the machine this site runs on and never here. If it is not set there, the description is complete and unusable.
takes.publicWhy: Neither the list nor a single manifest asks for a sign-in. The names of the key variables are taken out of that public answer. The addresses, the actions and everything they take are not.
takes.write: Only an owner may write one
takes.writeWhy: Set by AIMEAT_MSM_INSTALL_ROLE, which is owner unless the operator changed it. Deleting one is an owner's too.
takes.travelWhy: A manifest marked to travel goes to the sites this one is peered with, and any of them can also be packed into a component package and shipped anywhere.
takes.box: A manifest is a claim about somebody else's service. Nothing here checks that the address still answers, that the actions still exist, or that what they take and give back is still right. A manifest may even declare a health check, and nothing runs it. Nothing here has changed in {days} days.

detail.canAsk: What an AI can ask it to do
detail.noActions: It declares no actions, so there is nothing to ask it for.
detail.keyIn: This service wants a key, and the manifest says it is in
detail.keyWhy: This page cannot tell you whether that variable is set on the machine. If it is not, everything above is right and nothing can use it.
detail.keyNoneWhy: Anyone who can reach the address can call it.
detail.checkWhy: Either way nothing on this site runs one. Whether the address still answers, still has these actions, and still gives back these fields is unknown here.
detail.whoSees: Who can see it, and what you can do
detail.readableWhy: The name of the key variable is taken out of that public answer. The address, the actions and everything they take are in it.
detail.federateOn: Marked to travel to the sites this one is peered with.
detail.descriptionLabel: The description an AI reads first
detail.editWhat: Only the description and whether it travels to peers. The address, the actions and the key it wants are the manifest itself: to change those, write it again and register the new one.

write.title: Write a new manifest
write.lead: You are describing an outside service so that an AI can call it. Nothing here will call it, and the service does not have to exist yet.
write.startFromWhy: Open one, change the address and the fields, and you have written yours.
write.yamlPlaceholder: version, service, auth, actions. Start from one above to see the shape.
write.federate: Send it to the sites this one is peered with
write.shapeCheckedWhy: That it parses, that the category and the auth type are words this site knows, and that every action has an id, an address and a method. One that fails is refused with the lines to fix.
write.serviceNotWhy: Nothing calls the address, nothing looks for the key, nothing runs the health block. A manifest for a service that was switched off last year saves exactly as cleanly.
write.goesPublic: It becomes public the moment it saves
write.goesPublicWhy: Anyone can read it without signing in. The name of the key variable is taken out of that answer; the address and the actions are not.

dialog.deleteWarn: The manifest goes and nothing here puts it back. Anything already built on it, and any agent that was told to read it, stops finding it.

cortex.intro: Cortex is the browser code an app loads. Installing one puts its pieces here, and turning it on serves them to every app that asks for them.

now.title: Right now
now.line: {n} installed, and {unused} of them are loaded by no app at all.
now.lineOff: {off} are switched off, and an app still asks for {breaking} of those.

strip.carryingSub: at least one app loads it

find.placeholder: Find by name, owner, tag or description

loaded.title: Loaded by apps
loaded.noMatch: Nothing here matches what you typed.
loaded.none: No app loads any of these yet.

unused.title: Loaded by nothing
unused.lead: No app here loads any of these. They are grouped by facts you can check rather than by name, so the leftovers of one app that is gone, the same thing installed twice, and the kit this site ships do not all read alike.
unused.none: Every cortex here is loaded by at least one app.

group.lookalike: {n} names that look like the same thing
group.sameLettersWhy: The same letters and digits, written with different punctuation. One is almost certainly a second install of the other.
group.containsWhy: One name sits inside the other, which usually means a rename that left the first one behind.
group.closeWhy: The names differ by a few letters. That can be a typo and it can be two real things, so read the descriptions before deciding.
group.batchWhy: Installed together in one sitting and loaded by nothing since. Usually the parts of one app that is no longer published.
group.siteWhy: This site installed these itself so that anyone building an app can reach for them. Nothing has asked yet, they cost nothing to leave on, and leaving them alone is the right move.
group.oneWhy: Installed {when} by {who}. Nothing else here looks like it.

off.title: What turning one off does
off.goes: Off takes its pieces back out
off.goesWhy: Its shapes, instructions, actions, boards and word lists are taken out, and its files stop being served. An app that loads it breaks the next time somebody opens it, with no warning to them.
off.stays: The files and the data it wrote stay put
off.staysWhy: Turning it back on puts everything back where it was. That is why off is the safe move: you can take it back.
off.remove: Remove for good cannot be taken back
off.removeWhy: It deletes the cortex and its files. Nothing puts them back, so it asks you to type the name first.

read.title: Who can read the insides
read.lead: Every cortex here is in exactly one of these three, and they answer one question: who besides you may read its pieces, instructions and files. The first two are the word its owner chose, and the third overrides that word. None of it decides whether the cortex runs.
read.publicWhy: Anyone signed in here can read it. That is how a person builds an app on somebody else's kit.
read.privateWhy: The person who installed it, and you. Nobody else, not even by guessing the name.
read.siteWhy: Readable by everyone whatever word is on it, because this is the site's own kit and every app is meant to build on it. Some of these are marked public and some private, and here that makes no difference.
read.box: You see all {n} because you are the operator. A person signed in as themselves sees the public ones, this site's own, and their own. The count on their screen is a different number, and that is correct.

piece.schemaWhy: Says what a saved record has to look like. This site checks it against every memory key matching
piece.schemaPlain: Says what a saved record has to look like.
piece.promptWhy: A written instruction an app can ask for, so the AI helping someone knows what this can do.
piece.actionWhy: Something an app can ask this site to run on its behalf.
piece.boardWhy: A board this site set up when the extension was turned on.
piece.ontologyWhy: A list of agreed words, so two apps mean the same thing by the same term.
piece.seedWhy: Turning it on wrote these into memory. They are somebody's data now, not the extension's:
piece.seedNone: It would write starting data into memory, and has written none.
piece.libWhy: Served to any browser that asks for it, and gives the app
piece.libPlain: Served to any browser that asks for it.
piece.otherWhy: A piece this page does not have a word for yet.

detail.nobodyWhy: No app here has ever asked for it. Either it was built for something that is gone, or the app meant to use it was never published.
detail.nobodySite: No app here has ever asked for it. It ships with this site so that anyone building an app can reach for it, which is a reason to leave it on even while nothing uses it.
detail.put: What it put on this site
detail.noPieces: It has no pieces at all, so turning it on does nothing.
detail.keeps: The shapes, instructions and files go, right away. Anything it wrote into memory stays where it is, and so would removing it for good. Data this site wrote on somebody's behalf belongs to them, and no switch here takes it back.
detail.noVersions: No copies were kept, so there is nothing to go back to.
detail.olderOne: An older copy, still served to anything that asks for it by name.
detail.versionsWhy: Every install keeps a copy of what it installed. An app may ask for a version by name and keeps getting exactly that one after you install a newer, which is why an old copy is worth keeping rather than tidying away.
detail.canWhy: Off is a decision you can take back. Removing is not, so it asks you to type the name first.

dialog.offBreaks: They stop getting it the moment you press the button. The next person to open one of them meets a broken page, and nothing tells them why.
dialog.offNobody: No app here loads this one, so nothing breaks today.
dialog.goesWhy: Its shapes, instructions, actions and boards, and the files it serves to a browser.
dialog.staysWhy: The files themselves and everything it has written. Turning it back on puts all of it back.
dialog.offDoForOne: Turn it off for one app
dialog.removeWarn: The cortex and its files go, and nothing here puts them back. Anything it wrote into somebody's memory stays, because that is their data rather than this extension's.
dialog.batchTitle: Remove this whole group for good?
dialog.batchAsk: All {n} of these go, one after the other. No app here loads any of them.
dialog.batchWarn: Nothing puts them back. If one of them refuses, the rest still go, and you are told how many of each.

prompts.intro: The instructions this site gives an AI when it asks what it may do here. Every one of them can be read, changed, switched off, and put back to the version the software ships now.
prompts.took: Done. This prompt is the version the software ships now.
prompts.tookGroup: {n} prompts in {group} are now the versions the software ships. {on} that were switched off are on again, and {langs} lost a translation.
prompts.tookAll: Every prompt is back to the version the software ships, and the version histories are gone.
prompts.switchedOff: Switched off. Nobody is served this prompt now.
prompts.takeOneAsk: Replace "{name}" with the version the software ships now? Your text stays in the version list.
prompts.takeDropsLanguages: The translations of this prompt go with it.
prompts.takeGroupAsk: Replace all {n} prompts in {group} with the versions the software ships now? Each one keeps its own history, any that are switched off come back on, and their translations go.
prompts.takeAllAsk: Replace EVERY prompt on this site with the version the software ships, and delete every version history? Nothing can be brought back from this page afterwards.
prompts.switchOffAsk: Switch off "{name}"? It is then served to nobody: whoever asks for it is told it is not available.
prompts.versionsLead: Every save and every take is kept, the last fifty of them. Put one back and it becomes the text in use.
prompts.versionsNone: This prompt has not been changed here yet.
prompts.restoreAsk: Put version {v} back as the text in use?
prompts.notePh: What did you change? One line, kept with the version.
prompts.pickOne: Choose a prompt on the left to read it.

now.lineFactory: {n} prompts, every one of them the text the software ships.
now.lineEdited: {n} prompts. {changed} have been changed here, and {code} of those will be replaced at the next update.
now.noChange: nothing has been changed here yet
now.yoursRow: Changed here, and yours to keep
now.yoursWhy: The software never writes over a prompt you have changed. Taking the current version is how a newer text gets into one of these, one prompt or a whole group at a time. A prompt nobody has changed here takes the newer text at the next update on its own.
now.codeRow: Changed here, but the software wins
now.codeWhy: These follow the code: at the next update the shipped text is written over yours, and your version stays only in the history.
now.orphanRow: Not in the software any more
now.orphanWhy: Seeded by an older version and kept ever since. Still served exactly as stored, and there is no current version to take.
now.offWhy: A prompt that is off is not served at all: whoever asks for it is told it is not available.
now.langWhy: A reader who asks in that language gets it. The rest answer in English.

strip.promptsSub: an AI can be handed here
strip.orphanSub: the software no longer ships them

prompts.searchPh: Search {n} prompts: a name, an address, or the text itself
prompts.takeGroup: Take the current versions for these {n}

kind.yours: Yours to keep once you change it. Until then, an update brings the newer text; after a change, no update writes over it.
kind.code: Follows the code: the next update writes the shipped text over yours, and yours stays in the version list.
kind.orphan: The software no longer ships this one. It is served exactly as stored, and there is no current version to take.

prompts.textLabel: The text an AI is given
prompts.textHint: The names in double brackets are filled in when the prompt is handed out. A name this prompt does not declare is handed to the AI exactly as you typed it, brackets and all, which is why the declared names are listed above.
prompts.langLabel: In {language}, when the reader asks in {language}
prompts.langPh: Leave it empty and a {language} reader gets the English above.
prompts.langHint: The reader's own request decides: the exact language first, then the language without the country. Taking the current version drops every translation of that prompt.

taking.title: Taking the current version
taking.lead: The software keeps improving these texts. Taking the current version is how a newer one gets into use here, one prompt or one whole group at a time. It is the everyday button on this page, and it sits where a hand reaches.
taking.writes: It writes the text this site ships now
taking.writesWhy: Your own text goes into the version list in the same move, so it can be undone.
taking.languages: It drops the translations with it
taking.languagesWhy: The Finnish or Spanish text of that prompt goes when the English is replaced. Copy it out first, or write it again after.
taking.group: A whole group also switches everything in it back on
taking.groupWhy: It touches every prompt in the group, whether you changed it or not, and any prompt you had switched off is switched on again.
taking.orphan: A prompt the software no longer ships has nothing to take
taking.orphanWhy: It is served exactly as stored, for good. The button is not offered for those, rather than offered and refused.
taking.dangerLabel: The one button that is not safe
taking.danger: Taking the current version for every prompt does the whole site at once AND clears every version history with it. After that nothing can be brought back from this page. One prompt and one group both keep their histories, which is why they are the buttons that sit where you work.
taking.takeAll: Take the current version for every prompt

database.waitHourly: the first one goes in when this starts up

metrics.title: Metrics
metrics.disabled: The metrics endpoint is switched off on this node.
metrics.disabledHint: Set this in the node's environment and restart:
metrics.denied: Metrics are operator-only on this node, and this session lacks the operator role.
metrics.ledgerIntro: Reserved from the operating system counts every page lent to this process, including ones the program already freed and the C allocator kept for reuse. It is not a measure of what is in use, which is why a big number there reads as a leak and is not one. The number to watch is memory in actual use.
metrics.ledgerJsHint: Live objects the code is using right now.
metrics.ledgerHeadroomHint: Space V8 reserved in advance and is not using yet.
metrics.ledgerExternalHint: File buffers and WASM sandboxes outside the JS heap. Rises while jobs run, falls when they finish.
metrics.ledgerOtherHint: Native library memory, plus pages the program already freed that the allocator keeps for reuse instead of returning to the operating system. Free to the program, still counted by the OS.
metrics.ledgerRssHint: The measured one: the operating system’s own count for this process. The three rows above it are measured too, and the fourth is the remainder, so the column adds up by construction.
metrics.needsTwoSamples: rate appears after the second poll
metrics.chartNote: one reading per 10 s · nothing survives a reload
metrics.chartWait: The line needs two readings. The next one lands in ten seconds, and the page keeps them for as long as it stays open.
metrics.routesLead: Counted since the process started, so the share is of every call it has answered. Per second is measured between the last two readings, ten seconds apart.
metrics.routesShown: {n} routes shown, the busiest first. They carry {calls} of the {total} calls since boot.
metrics.routesNote: method and route together: a GET and a POST to one path are different work
metrics.refusedLead: Three counters that only ever rise. A number here is not a fault on its own; a number that climbs while nothing changed is the one to look at.
metrics.refAuth: Refused for want of a credential
metrics.refAuthWhy: Every 401 this process answered: a token that did not verify, and also a request that carried nothing at all. On a public address most of it is the open internet knocking.
metrics.refRateWhy: A caller went over what its door allows and got a 429. Usually one agent in a loop, and the tier it hit is on the sample.
metrics.refScopeWhy: An agent asked for something its scopes do not cover. Counted at the 403 that refuses a scope.
metrics.allLead: The same text a Prometheus scraper reads, one row per sample. Everything above is drawn from this; type a word to find the rest.
metrics.allNote: the name and version of this installation are on every sample and are dropped here

subdomains.title: Subdomains

subdomains.refuseTaken: A name a mapping already holds

subdomains.refuseNoApp: A target no published app matches
