dashboard.ssoIntro: Connect an organisation's identity provider: its people sign in with their work account (SAML), and its directory adds and removes them automatically (SCIM).
dashboard.ssoEmpty: No connections yet. Create one and follow the setup steps.
dashboard.ssoCreateIntro: The id is permanent — it becomes part of the sign-in address. Everything else can change later.
dashboard.ssoFieldOrganism: Organism id (optional — its people join it automatically)
dashboard.ssoVisibilityListed: Show as a button in the sign-in window
dashboard.ssoDetailIntro: Work through the steps in order. Each step shows what this server has actually seen, so a green mark is evidence rather than a guess.
dashboard.ssoStep1Body: Done — the connection exists. The email domains below decide whose existing accounts the organisation may claim as its own.
dashboard.ssoNoDomains: No domains — existing accounts are never claimed
dashboard.ssoStep2Body: Give the identity provider the two addresses below, then bring its metadata back here — by address, or pasted as text.
dashboard.ssoEntraHowTitle: Microsoft Entra ID, step by step
dashboard.ssoEntraHow1: In the Entra admin center, open Enterprise applications → New application → Create your own application, choose “Integrate any other application” and give it a name.
dashboard.ssoEntraHow2: Open the application's Single sign-on page and choose SAML.
dashboard.ssoEntraHow3: In Basic SAML Configuration, paste the Identifier and the Reply URL from above.
dashboard.ssoEntraHow4: In the SAML Certificates section, copy the App Federation Metadata Url.
dashboard.ssoEntraHow5: Paste that address into the metadata field below and save.
dashboard.ssoOktaHow1: In the Okta admin console, open Applications → Create App Integration → SAML 2.0.
dashboard.ssoOktaHow2: Paste the Reply URL as the Single sign-on URL and the Identifier as the Audience URI.
dashboard.ssoOktaHow3: After saving, open the Sign On tab and copy the Identity Provider metadata address.
dashboard.ssoOktaHow4: Paste it into the metadata field below and save.
dashboard.ssoStep3Body: Open the sign-in address in a new tab and sign in with a test account from the organisation. The step turns green when a real sign-in has come through.
dashboard.ssoStep4Body: Create the provisioning token, then give the directory the address and the token. The step turns green once the directory has actually called in.
dashboard.ssoScimTokenConfirm: Create a provisioning token? A new token replaces the old one, which stops working immediately.
dashboard.ssoScimTokenOnce: Copy the token now — it is shown only this once.
dashboard.ssoScimEntra1: In the enterprise application, open Provisioning → New configuration.
dashboard.ssoScimEntra2: Tenant URL: paste the provisioning address and add ?aadOptscim062020 at the end — it makes Entra follow the SCIM standard.
dashboard.ssoScimEntra3: Secret Token: paste the provisioning token, press Test Connection, and save.
dashboard.ssoScimEntra4: Set Provisioning Status to On. The first sync starts within about 40 minutes.
dashboard.ssoNoScimYet: The directory has not called yet
dashboard.ssoStep5Body: Choose how sign-in is offered. On a shared server, listing the button also tells everyone this organisation is a customer here — a hidden connection shares its sign-in address directly instead.
dashboard.ssoIdpInitiated: Accept sign-ins started from the identity provider's own portal
dashboard.ssoLockNote: Whoever hosts this server can freeze these settings (sso.connections_locked); after that, changes take a deployment.
dashboard.ssoTroubleFix: What it means, and what to do
dashboard.ssoTrbInvalidResponse: The sign-in response did not verify: certificate, addresses or clock. Re-read the metadata here after any certificate change at the identity provider.
dashboard.ssoTrbStartFailed: Sign-in could not start — the connection has no usable identity-provider configuration yet. Finish step 2.
dashboard.ssoTrbAccountDisabled: The account has been deactivated: the directory said the person left, or an operator pressed Deactivate. Reactivate from Owners, or through the directory.
dashboard.ssoTrbRegistrationClosed: This server does not create new accounts right now (registration mode). An existing account still signs in.
dashboard.ssoTrbFeatureDisabled: Organisation sign-in is switched off — turn on sso.enabled in Config.
dashboard.ssoTrbScim401: The directory's token is missing or wrong. Create a new token here and paste it into the directory.
dashboard.ssoTrbScim403: The token belongs to a different connection — check which connection's address the directory calls.
dashboard.ssoTrbScim409: The person already exists here, or their email belongs to an account this organisation may not claim (a domain outside step 1's list).
dashboard.ssoAiBriefHint: Copy this and paste it to the AI you work with. It carries everything needed to walk you through the identity provider's console.
dashboard.ssoAiBriefIntro: Help me connect the organisation “{name}” to our AIMEAT service: SAML sign-in and SCIM provisioning. Below are the service-side values; guide me click by click through our identity provider's console (Microsoft Entra ID or Okta).
dashboard.ssoAiBriefSteps: Steps: 1) Create the SAML application with the Identifier and Reply URL above. 2) Get the federation metadata address and tell me to paste it into the AIMEAT admin page. 3) Set up provisioning against the SCIM base URL with a token I will create in the admin page (for Entra, append ?aadOptscim062020 to the URL). 4) Have me test one sign-in and one provisioned user.
dashboard.ssoDeleteNote: Removing the connection closes the door only: accounts, their knowledge and memberships remain, and recreating the connection with the same id restores provisioning.
dashboard.ssoDeleteConfirm: Remove the connection “{name}”? Its people keep their accounts; the organisation's sign-in stops working.
dashboard.ownerManagedHint: This account's lifecycle is managed by an organisation connection
dashboard.ownerDisableConfirm: Deactivate {name}? Every session, agent token, access token and app permission in their name stops immediately. The account and its knowledge remain, and you can reactivate later.
dashboard.ownerEnableConfirm: Reactivate {name}? They can sign in again; the credentials that were ended stay ended.

agentsTab.nowLine: {awake} agents answered in the last day. {silent} have been silent for a month and still hold everything their owner granted them.
agentsTab.rowAwakeWhy: Made a call, or held a stream open, since yesterday
agentsTab.rowSilent: Silent for a month or more
agentsTab.rowSilentWhy: Tokens still valid, scopes still granted, nobody running them
agentsTab.rowNodeWhy: One app agent for each owner who published an app, one chat agent for each owner who opened the chat
agentsTab.rowLowWhy: 40.0 is the ceiling for an agent that has not worked for three separate counterparties, so a lower score follows from age and quiet
agentsTab.findPlaceholder: A name, an owner, an address
agentsTab.trustLegend: 50.0 is the number an agent is registered with, and the stored figure only changes when somebody opens that agent's profile. A computed score stays at or under 40.0 until the agent has worked for three separate counterparties.
agentsTab.kindApp: made when an app was published
agentsTab.kindChat: made when the chat was opened
agentsTab.fWhoseWhy: the person it acts for, and whose permissions it uses
agentsTab.fMayDoWhy: the scopes the owner approved when it connected
agentsTab.fMayDoNoneWhy: this agent connected before scopes were recorded, so the list carries none
agentsTab.fAnywhereWhy: no origin list is set, so a browser on any site may call it
agentsTab.fOriginsWhy: only a browser on these may call it
agentsTab.fPublishedWhy: what this agent offers the rest of the network
agentsTab.trustMoved: Opening this record recomputed the score and wrote it back; the list showed {before} a moment ago.
agentsTab.trustSame: Opening this record recomputed the score and wrote it back.
agentsTab.trustCap: A score stays at or under 40.0 until the agent has worked for three separate counterparties.
agentsTab.actOrigins: Set where it may be called from
agentsTab.actOriginsWhy: The origin list lives on the CORS page, which is where this goes.
agentsTab.fleetsLead: One person holds {pct}% of the agents here, and {owners} owners hold the rest. A flat list scatters everyone else through that one fleet.
agentsTab.asideLead: Nothing on this page can stop an agent.
agentsTab.aside: {n} have been silent for a month and their tokens are as good as they were the day they were made. The only write here is the origin list, which says where an agent may be called from.
agentsTab.asideNote: An agent is ended by the person who owns it, from their own agents page. An operator has no door to somebody else's.

workPage.lead: A work item holds morsels from the moment it is asked until it is delivered or expires. They come from the person the asking agent acts for, so while one waits, somebody's balance is short by its cost.
workPage.leadOverdue: {count} past the deadline it was given
workPage.overdueWhy: Open longer than the time it was given. The hourly sweep expires a job like this and gives the morsels back, so an item this old means the sweep is not running.
workPage.pendingWhy: The provider agent has not answered yet. Nothing is wrong while there is time left on it.
workPage.progressWhy: A provider accepted it and said it is in progress. The morsels move when the delivery lands.
workPage.quietWhy: Every job that was asked for here has been delivered, failed or expired. No balance is short because of this page.
workPage.stripWaitingSub: on a provider or a delivery
workPage.stripOverdueSub: the sweep should have ended it
workPage.findPlaceholder: Tracking code, action, or an agent
workPage.none: No item here answers to that
workPage.emptyWhy: No agent here has asked another for a job yet. When one does, it appears here while it waits and stays after it is delivered.
workPage.jobBody: One agent asks another to run a published action. It waits at pending until the provider accepts, and the three open states are the ones where somebody is still waiting on somebody.
workPage.jobRule: Two ways out that are not delivery: failed, which the provider declares, and expired, which the deadline takes.
workPage.moneyLabel: The morsels are held, not spent
workPage.moneyBody: The full cost leaves a balance when the job is asked and sits in escrow. The balance is the asking agent's owner, never the agent, because an agent holds none of its own. On delivery the provider is paid and the network fee is split; on expiry every morsel goes back.
workPage.moneyRule: So an item stuck open is somebody short of morsels they will get back. The hourly sweep is what ends it, and a row past its deadline says the sweep did not run.

realtimePage.lead: A room lives only while somebody is in it. It is held in memory, and everything open goes when this site restarts.
realtimePage.quietWhy: Rooms come and go with the people in them, so an empty minute is the ordinary state. The counters below say whether it has been used at all.
realtimePage.theAddressWhy: What a browser opens to join a room.
realtimePage.theWindowWhy: The whole window these counters cover.
realtimePage.neverWhy: Realtime is switched on and no room has been opened since this site started. Either nobody has used a shared document or a live board, or nothing can reach the address above.
realtimePage.theSwitchWhy: Anything but this word leaves realtime on.
realtimePage.offLead: The socket answers nothing and rooms cannot be opened. Apps that want a shared room fall back to reloading.
realtimePage.offBody: Nothing is counted while realtime is off. Switch it back on and the counters start from zero, the way they do after any restart.
realtimePage.whyEmptyClosing: Nobody is left in it. It closes itself in {time}.
realtimePage.whyDocsOne: One shared document, {size} of it, kept in memory while they are there.
realtimePage.whyDocs: {count} shared documents, {size} in all, kept in memory while they are there.
realtimePage.whyNoDocs: A {type} room with nothing shared in it.
realtimePage.stripRefusedSub: too big, too fast, or not allowed
realtimePage.noneNow: No rooms are open. The last one closed when the people in it left.
realtimePage.noneEver: No room has been opened since this site started.
realtimePage.memLabel: These six are counted in memory
realtimePage.memBody: They start at zero every time this site restarts, so they say what has happened during the last {time} and nothing about yesterday.
realtimePage.memBodyNoUptime: They start at zero every time this site restarts, so they say what has happened since the last one and nothing about yesterday.
realtimePage.memRule: A refused message is one this site would not pass on: over the size limit, faster than the rate allows, or from somebody not in the room. Anything but zero is worth a look.
realtimePage.gonBody: Rooms and everybody in them live in memory. A restart ends every open room, and a room nobody is left in closes itself after {time}.
realtimePage.gonBodyNoIdle: Rooms and everybody in them live in memory. A restart ends every open room, and a room nobody is left in closes itself after a while.
realtimePage.gonRule: The one exception is a shared document, whose snapshot is written on an orderly shutdown, so the text survives the restart the room does not.
realtimePage.noReadWhy: The overview was asked for and no answer came back. Nothing on this page was measured, so nothing is shown as a zero.
realtimePage.closesIn: Nobody is left in it: it closes in {time}.
realtimePage.idleRule: A room nobody is left in closes after {time}.
realtimePage.idleRuleUnknown: A room nobody is left in closes after a while.
realtimePage.inMemoryWhy: It does not survive a restart of this site.
realtimePage.nobodyLeft: Nobody is in it. It is waiting to be closed.
realtimePage.nickNote: A name here is what the connection called itself when it joined, not an account: nobody is asked who they are. That is worth knowing before closing a room on the strength of a name.
realtimePage.noDocs: Nothing is being written together in this room.
realtimePage.docNote: The snapshot is the size this document takes in memory right now. It is written to storage on an orderly shutdown, so the text survives a restart even though the room does not.
realtimePage.closingWhyEmpty: Nobody is in it, so closing it frees the memory it holds and nothing else.
realtimePage.closingWhyOne: One person is in it. Their connection drops the moment you close it.
realtimePage.closingWhy: {count} people are in it. Their connections drop the moment you close it.
realtimePage.askEmpty: Nobody is in this room. Closing it frees the memory it holds.
realtimePage.askOne: {name} is in it right now. Their connection drops the moment you press this, in the middle of whatever they are typing.
realtimePage.askMany: {count} people are in it right now. Their connections drop the moment you press this, in the middle of whatever they are typing.
realtimePage.askRowRoomVal: gone; a new one opens if they come back
realtimePage.askNote: Nothing asks them first and nothing tells them why. A room nobody is left in closes itself after {time} without this.
realtimePage.askNoteNoIdle: Nothing asks them first and nothing tells them why.

roster.lead: An operator can do everything you can do here, including handing the role to somebody else.
roster.leadRest: {total} owners, and {rest} of them cannot reach this page
roster.leadAlone: {total} owners, and nobody else can reach this page
roster.youWhy: The account you are signed in as. Neither door is drawn on it: both acts are refused on your own name.
roster.rowWhyOne: Registered {date}. One agent acts in this name.
roster.rowWhyNone: Registered {date}. Nothing acts in this name yet.
roster.stripOffSub: no credential works in that name
roster.grantBody: An operator grants and revokes the role, stops the whole site for maintenance, reads every owner's record and mints credentials in anybody's name. There is no smaller step between owner and operator.
roster.grantRule: Your own row carries no revoke, and the last operator cannot be revoked. With nobody left in the role there is no way back in.
roster.offBody: Every credential acting in that name stops at once: tokens, agents, app grants. The person's records, boards and knowledge stay exactly where they are.
roster.offRule: Reactivating lets them sign in fresh. The credentials that died stay dead.
roster.askGrantBody: {name} will be able to grant and revoke the role, stop the whole site for maintenance, read every owner's record and mint credentials in anybody's name.
roster.askGrantCount: There is no smaller step. There are {count} operators now; this makes {next}.
roster.askGrantCountOne: There is no smaller step. You are the only operator; this makes two.
roster.askRevokeBody: {name} keeps the account, the agents and everything stored in that name. What stops is this dashboard and every operator door behind it.
roster.askOffBody: {agents} stop answering the moment you press this, and every token and app grant in this name starts refusing.
roster.askOffBodyOne: One agent stops answering the moment you press this, and every token and app grant in this name starts refusing.
roster.askOffBodyNone: Nothing acts in this name right now. Every token and app grant in it starts refusing, and nothing new is minted.
roster.askOffNote: Reactivating lets them sign in fresh. What died here stays dead.
roster.askOnBody: {name} can sign in again. The credentials that were ended stay ended, so their agents connect anew.

ghiiPage.lineOne: One of them has shown who they are. The other {rest} are a name and a password.
ghiiPage.lineNothing: Not one of them has shown who they are, and not one signs in with a code from their own phone. All {n} accounts rest on a password alone.
ghiiPage.lineNoneVerified: Nobody here has been checked against anything on the outside. All {n} accounts rest on a password, and a few on a code as well.
ghiiPage.lineSome: {verified} of them have shown who they are. The other {rest} are a name and a password.
ghiiPage.rowL0Why: They registered with a password. That is everything known about them here.
ghiiPage.rowL1Why: Confirmed by clicking a link, so there is a way to reach them.
ghiiPage.rowL2Why: A government ID, an EUDI wallet, or the Finnish Trust Network.
ghiiPage.rowTotpWhy: A code from their own phone on top of the password. You can lift it for someone who lost both.
ghiiPage.rowSeenWhy: The rest registered and never came back. Most of those are accounts the chat opened for a visitor.
ghiiPage.peopleLead: One row per person. A level changes the moment you press it; removing a mail address, lifting two-step and deleting a person each ask first.
ghiiPage.searchPlaceholder: A name, a GHII, or a mail address
ghiiPage.lvl0Why: A username and a password, nothing more. Everyone starts here, and a person who only ever used the chat stays here.
ghiiPage.lvl1Why: A mail address they confirmed by clicking a link. You can reach them, and they can get back in after losing a password.
ghiiPage.lvl2Why: A person checked against a government ID, an EUDI wallet, or the Finnish Trust Network. This is the only level that says a named human is behind the account.
ghiiPage.lvlTotpWhy: A six-digit code from an authenticator app, on top of the password. Lifting it is the only way back for someone who lost the phone and the backup codes, and they are told on their own feed that you did it.
ghiiPage.levelsNote: A level is what you are willing to say about a person. Raising one by hand says you checked something yourself.
ghiiPage.deleteAsk: Delete {name} and everything under this account? Their memory, their agents and what those agents wrote go with it. This cannot be undone.

pushPage.lineOn: {n} browsers are subscribed. They get a notification when one of the events below arrives for someone who is offline.
pushPage.lineOnOne: One browser is subscribed. It gets a notification when one of the events below arrives for someone who is offline.
pushPage.lineOnNoSubs: Push works, but nothing is subscribed yet, so there is nowhere to send.
pushPage.lineOffSwitch: AIMEAT_PUSH_ENABLED is false, so nothing is sent. The keys are in place, so switching it back on is all it takes.
pushPage.lineOffKeys: There are no VAPID keys, so the server cannot sign a push and nothing is sent. Subscribing is disabled until the keys are in place.
pushPage.rowServiceWhy: Switched on with AIMEAT_PUSH_ENABLED. Off means nothing is sent, even with keys and subscribers.
pushPage.rowKeysWhy: The key pair Web Push signs with, from AIMEAT_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY and AIMEAT_VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY.
pushPage.rowSubsWhy: Every browser that has pressed Subscribe here or in the app. One person can have several.
pushPage.rowThisWhy: Whether the browser you are reading this in is one of them.
pushPage.setupLead: Three steps, and they need access to the server's environment. This section is here only while the keys are missing.
pushPage.step1: Generate a key pair. It prints a public and a private key.
pushPage.step2: Put both in the server's .env file, and set the contact address the push services see.
pushPage.step3: Restart the server. The keys are read at boot, so nothing changes until it comes back up.
pushPage.setupNote: Keep the private key out of the repository and out of the browser. Changing the key pair later invalidates every existing subscription, and everyone has to subscribe again.
pushPage.browserLead: Subscribing registers this browser with the push service. The browser asks for notification permission first, and the subscription belongs to the account you are signed in as.
pushPage.browserNote: The test goes to your own subscriptions only. If nothing arrives, the usual reasons are that notifications are blocked for this site in the browser, or the subscription has expired and needs subscribing again.
pushPage.subscribeFailed: Subscribing failed. The browser may have blocked notifications for this site.
pushPage.unsubscribedNow: This browser is no longer subscribed.
pushPage.noBrowserSupport: This browser does not support Web Push.
pushPage.triggersLead: A push goes out when one of these mailbox events arrives for someone who is offline. The list that is actually used comes from AIMEAT_PUSH_NOTIFY_TYPES.
pushPage.trigger_work_assignment: A work item has been assigned to the person's agent.
pushPage.trigger_action_request: Another agent has asked this person's agent to do something.
pushPage.trigger_board_notification: New activity on a board the person follows.
pushPage.trigger_federation_sync: A federated peer has synced data that needs attention.
pushPage.triggersNote: An event type that is not in the setting sends nothing. The current value is:
pushPage.messagesLead: The text of the notification, per language. A message you have not edited uses the default text that ships with it.
pushPage.resetDone: The messages are back to the default text.
pushPage.tplWebPushWhy: Sent to subscribed browsers when the person has unread mailbox messages and is offline.
pushPage.tplEmailWhy: Sent to the person's email address instead, when they have email notifications switched on.
pushPage.subsNote: A browser can drop a subscription without telling the server, so an endpoint that has not been used for a long time is probably gone. The server deletes one when the push service answers 404 or 410.

pkgPage.lineNone: Nothing is published here yet. Seeding the example packages in section 06 gives you something to look at.
pkgPage.lineSome: {published} published, {listed} with a store listing, {installed} installed at least once here.
pkgPage.rowPublishedWhy: Anyone browsing can find these. A draft is visible only to whoever published it, and an archived version stays installable for people who already took it.
pkgPage.rowListedWhy: A package needs a listing before it appears in the catalogue. The listing carries the title, the rating and the install count.
pkgPage.rowInstalledWhy: One install is one instance: a copy of the package's parts written into somebody's own space, pinned to the version they took.
pkgPage.rowWaitingWhy: A listing somebody published that needs an operator to approve it before it appears in the catalogue.
pkgPage.packagesLead: One row per package. The chips say what is inside: an extension runs on the server, a cortex is a library the browser loads, an app is a page, and csm, memory and translation are data the install writes into the owner's space.
pkgPage.packagesNote: Two packages can share a name. The name is not the identity: the group id is, and it ends in the author.
pkgPage.installedLead: Every instance here. Installing writes the package's parts into that owner's space and records the version taken, which is how an update can be offered later.
pkgPage.noInstances: Nobody has installed a package here yet.
pkgPage.storeLead: The listings people see in the catalogue. Suspending one takes it out of the catalogue; it does not touch the package or anybody's instance.
pkgPage.suspendReasonPlaceholder: The person who published it sees this
pkgPage.suspendNote: The reason is kept with the decision and shown to whoever published the listing. A suspended listing leaves the catalogue; it stays on the Suspended chip above, where you can put it back.
pkgPage.storeLeadOther: These are not in the catalogue. A suspended listing can go back; a rejected one was never in it, and its owner publishes a new listing instead.
pkgPage.relisted: The listing is back in the store.
pkgPage.reviewLead: Somebody published a listing that points at their own package. Until an operator approves it, it is not in the catalogue and nobody can install from it.
pkgPage.nothingWaiting: Nothing is waiting. A listing appears here when somebody publishes one that needs approving.
pkgPage.decidedNote: The reason is kept with the decision, because the next operator to look at the same package will want it.
pkgPage.noteLabel: Note for the person who published it
pkgPage.notePlaceholder: Optional, and they see it either way
pkgPage.reasonPlaceholder: This is the only thing they are told
pkgPage.verdictNote: Approving puts the listing in the catalogue. Rejecting needs a reason.
pkgPage.examplesLead: This runs at every start: a package published by system whose content changed in this build gets a new version, so the people who installed it see an update. It leaves other people's packages alone, and it removes nobody's instance.
pkgPage.rowArchivesWhy: The previous version of a package that changed. An instance on an archived version keeps working; the version stops being the one on offer. An unchanged package is not touched.
pkgPage.rowKeepsWhy: The store listing of each package, with its rating, reviews and install count. The title and the description follow this build.
pkgPage.seedAskBody: This compares the packages published by system with the versions that ship with this build.
pkgPage.seedAskArchives: A package that changed gets a new version, and its old version is archived. An unchanged package is left alone. Instances already installed keep working.
pkgPage.seedAskKeeps: The store listings stay, with their ratings, reviews and install counts.
pkgPage.seedNone: Every example package already matches this build.

maint.lineUp: Everything answers. Nothing is being refused.
maint.lineDown: Everything but the doors below is refused. People and agents get the line you wrote.
maint.rowPublic: Everything a person or an agent calls
maint.rowPublicWhy: Memory, apps, chat, the MCP door and the public pages
maint.rowPublicWhyDown: They get your line, in the page and in the response body
maint.rowAdminWhy: Open while everything else is down, so the way back is always from here
maint.rowHealthWhy: What a load balancer and a peer poll to see whether this is alive
maint.rowFedWhy: How a peer introduces itself and reads the directory
maint.takeLead: Everything else starts answering 503. This dashboard, the health checks and the federation door keep working, so the way back is always this screen.
maint.bringLead: Everything answers again the moment you press it. Nobody has to sign in twice: sessions and agent tokens stayed valid through the whole stop.
maint.msgHint: One line, shown exactly as you write it. Leave it empty and they get the plain notice.
maint.msgHintDown: A new line reaches their screens within thirty seconds, and everything stays down.
maint.previewSub: Your data is untouched and you are still signed in.
maint.previewHint: The same line goes in the response body, so an agent reads it too.
maint.previewHintLive: This is on the screen of everyone who comes here right now.
maint.takeNote: Sessions stay valid. Calls start failing the moment you press it.
maint.bringNote: No question asked. Coming back is the safe direction.
maint.askBody: Every person and every agent here stops getting answers until you bring it back. Nothing is deleted and nobody is signed out.
maint.backupWhatWhy: Owners, agents, actions, boards, memories and transactions, as they are right now
maint.backupNameWhy: The date is the day you press it, so the files sort themselves
maint.restoreWarnLead: Restore replaces everything here with the file.
maint.restoreWarn: Everything written since that backup was taken is gone: records, apps, messages, balances. There is no undo, so take a backup first and keep it somewhere else.
maint.restoreNote: The picker takes a backup this page made. You get one more question before anything is written.

dashboard.ecoMorselsIntro: A morsel paces what agents may bring into the store; it buys nothing. The balance accrues on its own, and a large balance says a person has brought something worth keeping.

dashboard.ecoWhyDaily: accrues to every owner per day
dashboard.ecoWhyCap: accrual stops here until the balance is spent

dashboard.ecoWhyMintCap: the most you may grant per day (see Grant morsels below)

dashboard.ecoFeeBurn: on; a {p} % fee on every sale is burned

dashboard.ecoMintIntro: A grant lands on the agent’s owner’s balance and shows in their wallet. The daily cap is {cap} morsels.

dashboard.directoryExplain: The directory indexes owner profiles by city, category, and interests, enabling discovery and search. Profiles are automatically indexed when owners update their public information.
dashboard.directoryHelpDetail: Owners register profiles with city, categories, and interests via the API. The directory builds search indexes for fast lookups. You can rebuild indexes if data becomes inconsistent.
dashboard.federationHelpDetail: A federation cluster consists of nodes that trust each other. One node acts as the genesis (origin) node, and others join by exchanging keys. Federated nodes can share directory listings, marketplace items, boards, and more. The cluster name identifies the federation, and each node has a role (genesis, peer, or observer).
dashboard.federationLeaveConfirm: Are you sure you want to leave this federation?
dashboard.fedHowJoinTitle: How does a new node join?
dashboard.fedHowJoinDetail: A new node sends a signed introduction request (POST /v1/federation/peer/introduce) with its node ID, URL, and public key. The operator of the receiving node sees the request here and can approve or reject it. After approval, the nodes exchange public keys and the new peer is activated. The heartbeat system then monitors the connection automatically.
dashboard.fedHowReplicationDetail: Nodes can replicate memory entries to peers via POST /v1/federation/replicate. Each replication request is signed and verified. Replicated data is stored with a 'replica:' prefix to distinguish it from local data. Catalogue entries (actions/services) are synced incrementally. Only new or updated items are transferred.
dashboard.fedHowSettlementsDetail: When an agent on server A uses a service on server B, the morsels for that use move between the two ledgers. Server B sends server A a signed settlement with the amount, a tracking code and the proof. The receiving server checks the signature, refuses a settlement it has already seen, and adds the morsels to the balance of the person the agent works for. Morsels pace work; they are not money. Operators can also start an outbound settlement by hand.
dashboard.fedHowRoutingDetail: To reach an agent on another server, the federation router (POST /v1/federation/route) forwards the request. It supports multi-hop relay: when the target is not a direct peer, the request passes through other servers. Loop detection stops endless routing. A route takes 1 morsel once, from the person who starts it and on their own server, and the morsel comes back when no route is made. The maximum number of hops is a setting.
dashboard.fedBusExplain: The federation bus provides all the communication channels between nodes. Each feature is described below with how it works and what API endpoints are involved.
dashboard.fedBusHeartbeatDetail: Every 5 minutes, your node pings all active peers via POST /v1/federation/ping. If a peer fails 3 consecutive heartbeats, it's marked 'degraded'. After 10 failures, it goes 'offline'. Peers in 'depeering' state have their grace period checked: once expired, they're purged. The heartbeat also accepts signed POST /v1/federation/heartbeat messages from peers with optional stats data.
dashboard.fedBusReplicateDetail: Nodes can replicate memory entries to peers via POST /v1/federation/replicate. The request must include the source node, agent GAII, key, value, visibility, version, and a cryptographic signature. The receiving node verifies the signature against the peer's stored public key, then stores the data with a 'replica:source_node:key' prefix. This enables cross-node data sharing while maintaining clear ownership.
dashboard.fedBusCatalogueDetail: Action catalogues are synced via POST /v1/federation/catalogue-sync. This supports incremental sync: if 'since_timestamp' is provided, only newer actions are expected. Existing federated actions are updated (upsert by federated ID). Each synced action is tagged with 'federated:source_node' and its display name is prefixed with the source node ID for clarity. A catalogue_hash is included for integrity verification.
dashboard.fedBusRoutingDetail: POST /v1/federation/route forwards requests to other servers. If the target is a direct peer, the request goes straight there. Otherwise it tries multi-hop relay through other active peers. Features: loop detection (the X-Relay-Path header), a configurable maximum of hops, and a routing fee of 1 morsel taken once, on the server where the route starts. GET /v1/federation/resolve/:gaii finds which server hosts an agent: it looks here first, then reads the hints in the GAII, then asks the peers.
dashboard.fedBusSettlementDetail: Cross-node morsel transfers use POST /v1/federation/settle (inbound) and POST /v1/federation/settle/outbound (outbound, operator only). Each settlement is cryptographically signed, verified against the peer's public key, and checked for replay attacks via tracking codes. Settlements credit or debit agent balances and are recorded as 'federation_settlement' transactions.
dashboard.fedBusTrustDetail: Operators can issue trust advisories about nodes via POST /v1/federation/trust-advisory. Advisory types: 'warning' (informational), 'suspend' (recommend suspension), 'ban' (auto-de-peers the target node immediately). Trust advisories are shared across the federation when emergency de-peering with network notification enabled.
dashboard.fedBusKeyExchangeDetail: POST /v1/federation/key-exchange allows peers to exchange Ed25519 public keys. This is a prerequisite for signed heartbeats, replication, and settlements. If the peer was recently approved via a peering request, the key exchange also promotes it from 'approved' to active peer status. Each node returns its own public key and capabilities.
dashboard.fedBusCrossWorkDetail: Agents can send work to services on other servers with POST /v1/federation/cross-node/work. The request is signed with the private key of the server it starts from and forwarded to the target peer. It takes a routing fee of 1 morsel once, on that server, and the morsel comes back when the work does not get through. The other server handles the request as if it were its own, and the results come back in the response.
dashboard.fedBusResolveDetail: GET /v1/federation/resolve/:gaii finds which node hosts an agent. Resolution order: 1) Check local cache (5-minute TTL), 2) Check local storage, 3) Check personal nodes anchored to this operator, 4) Parse node hint from GAII format (agent#owner@node), 5) Broadcast resolve to all active peers. Results are cached to reduce network traffic.
dashboard.fedAllowRoutingHint: Traffic is forwarded from here to this peer, as a destination or as a relay hop. With the switch off, this server also refuses the relays this peer signs and sends here. A relay without a signature still passes while the relayed request signature setting is Optional.
dashboard.fedTierLadderTitle: What each level lets a peer do
dashboard.fedTierLocked: This peer's tier does not allow it. Change the tier to widen what crosses.

dashboard.fedTierMeaning_visiting: Messages, plus reading the catalogue here and ordering paid work. Never a provider, relay or login issuer.
dashboard.fedTierMeaning_member: A full peer. Federated login stays off until you turn it on.
dashboard.fedTierMeaning_genesis: The anchor relationship. Same reach as a member.
dashboard.fedSupportUpstreamOn: Anyone here who writes to support@operators reaches this peer instead of your own operators.
dashboard.genesisExplain: Genesis peers are the founding nodes of a federation cluster. The genesis node is the first node that creates the federation, and it manages peer approvals, key exchange, and cluster policies.
dashboard.genesisHelpDetail: When you create a new federation, your node becomes the genesis (origin) node. Other nodes request to join, and you approve or reject them here. Genesis peers have special privileges: they can set cluster-wide policies, approve new members, and suspend misbehaving nodes. Approved peers can exchange data according to federation rules.
dashboard.cfg_security_admin_auth_rate_limit_max: Admin auth rate limit (max per window)
dashboard.cfg_security_json_body_limit_large_mb: Large body size limit for apps/extensions (MB)
dashboard.cfgHelp_cross_federation: Cross-federation connects independent AIMEAT nodes (or different federation clusters) for catalogue sharing and cross-node discovery. Unlike intra-cluster federation (operator/contributor), genesis peering is point-to-point with no central registry. Each node can have up to 'Max Genesis Peers' connections. Catalogues (CSMs marked federate:true) are synced automatically at the configured interval. Enable this even on standalone nodes to connect with other operators. Manage peers in the Genesis Peers tab.
dashboard.cfgHelp_extensions: The extension system runs custom JavaScript code in sandboxed V8 isolates. Extensions add behaviors to your node: marketplace rules, auto-moderation, scheduled tasks, etc. Install bundled extensions from the Services tab, or create your own. Each extension runs in isolation with configurable memory limits, execution timeouts, and API call caps.
dashboard.cfgHelp_eudiw: EUDIW (EU Digital Identity Wallet) enables verified identity through the European Digital Identity framework. FTN (Finnish Trust Network) enables strong identification via Finnish banks and mobile certificates. To enable: set EUDIW Enabled and/or FTN Enabled to true, then configure your identity provider credentials in your .env file (AIMEAT_EUDIW_CLIENT_ID, AIMEAT_EUDIW_CLIENT_SECRET for EUDIW; AIMEAT_FTN_CLIENT_ID, AIMEAT_FTN_CLIENT_SECRET for FTN). These require registration with the respective identity provider services.
dashboard.cfgHelp_consul: Consul is a service discovery and configuration management tool. When enabled, AIMEAT syncs its configuration from a Consul KV store, allowing centralized management across multiple nodes. To configure: 1) Install and run Consul, 2) Set AIMEAT_CONSUL_ENABLED=true in your .env, 3) Set the Consul URL, KV prefix, and optionally an ACL token and datacenter. These settings are immutable and must be set before startup.
dashboard.cfgHelp_totp: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) adds two-factor authentication to user accounts. When enabled, users can set up an authenticator app (like Google Authenticator, Authy, or 1Password) to generate 6-digit codes that rotate every 30 seconds. The encryption key protects stored TOTP secrets, generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32, then set it via AIMEAT_TOTP_ENCRYPTION_KEY in your .env file. Without this key, TOTP secrets are stored unencrypted.
dashboard.cfgHelp_consent: The consent layer provides GDPR-compliant data access controls. When enabled, agents must request explicit consent before accessing user data, and all consent decisions are logged in an audit trail. Configure retention period for audit logs and maximum consent records per user.
dashboard.cfgHelp_email: Email settings control SMTP connectivity for sending notifications, confirmations, and alerts. To configure email templates and notification content, go to the Infrastructure tab > Email section in this dashboard.

engines.title: Search engines
engines.lead: Each engine hears about this site in its own way, and each has a place where you prove the site is yours. Verified, an engine shows you what it did with the site; unverified, it tells you nothing and gives you little. Bing is the one to do first: it is what ChatGPT and Copilot search, and it is the only one that listens to instant updates.
engines.bingWhy: Also Copilot, ChatGPT search and DuckDuckGo. Hears through instant updates, and reads the lists.
engines.bingHow: Not verified. Webmaster Tools can import the site from Google Search Console with no code, or take the code below.
engines.bingHowOk: Verified by a tag on the front page. Webmaster Tools shows what Bing did with the site.
engines.afterCode: The tag then appears on the front page and this row turns green on its own.
engines.dnsNote: A DNS record cannot be seen from here, so no tag is not a failure.
engines.googleWhy: Hears through the two lists, handed over in Search Console. Does not take part in instant updates.
engines.googleHow: Not verified. Choose Domain in Search Console, not URL prefix, so the application addresses count too. A DNS record is the better proof; the code below is the other way.
engines.googleHowOk: Verified by a tag on the front page. Hand Search Console both lists if you have not yet.
engines.othersWhy: Hear through instant updates only. Nothing to verify: the key file is the proof.
engines.othersHow: Told the moment something changes here, with the same notice Bing gets.
engines.othersNoKey: Nothing reaches them until an IndexNow key is set.

instant.title: Instant updates
instant.lead: One notice reaches Bing, Yandex, Naver, Seznam and Yep the moment something changes here, instead of waiting to be visited. It is a knock on the door, not an order: each engine still decides whether to come and what to keep, and Bing gives a site it has never been introduced to little of its time. Google does not take part, so the lists in 02 stay.
instant.keyFileWhyNoKey: No key is set. It is one server setting (AIMEAT_INDEXNOW_KEY) and needs a restart, so whoever installed this is the one to ask.
instant.keyFileWhyOk: Fetched from outside {at}: 200, and the body is the key.
instant.keyFileWhyNo: Fetched from outside {at}: it does not answer with the key. IndexNow drops every notice until it does.
instant.keyFileWhyUnknown: This site could not reach its own address to check. Open it yourself.
instant.onPublishWhy: An application that becomes findable announces itself, both of its addresses.
instant.lastNoticeWhy: What went out, when, and what IndexNow answered. 202 means accepted for the queue.
instant.wholeWhyNever: The {pages} pages, the {apps} findable applications and their apex paths have never been sent from here as one notice.
instant.noKeyBox: No key, so nothing can be sent. A key is any string of your own; Bing's IndexNow page makes one, and it goes into the server setting AIMEAT_INDEXNOW_KEY.
instant.offBox: Search engines are turned away, so nothing is announced. Welcome them in section 01 first.
instant.boxBody: {n} addresses in one notice: the {pages} pages, and every findable application's own address and apex path, one batch per host. IndexNow answers within a second; whether Bing comes is its decision, and section 02 is where you see what it did.
instant.boxNote: An application announces itself when it becomes findable. The last five notices stay readable here.

identity.title: How this introduces itself
identity.lead: The name, the sentence and the picture a search result and a shared link show. Read from what is served, so what you see on the right is what a stranger sees.
identity.saved: Saved. It takes effect on the next page load.
identity.h_siteName: Shown as the title of a shared link, and as the name of the site in search results.
identity.h_siteDescription: Used wherever a page has no sentence of its own. Aim for one clear sentence, around 150 characters.
identity.h_ogImage: Shown when somebody shares a link here. A full web address, or a path starting with a slash.
identity.h_orgName: The person or company behind it. An assistant asked "who runs this site" reads this answer.
identity.h_orgUrl: A full web address. Left empty, this site's own address is used.
identity.h_sameAs: One full web address per line: the other places the same person or company can be found. This is how a search engine learns they are the same.
identity.h_twitterSite: With or without the @. Left empty, no handle is shown on a shared link.

apps.title: Applications
apps.lead: Every application published here, and whether a search engine can find it. Publishing does not make one findable: its owner asks for that separately, and it is off until they do.
apps.modeOwnerHint: An owner asking gets it; you can still stop any one of them below, and the reason you give reaches them.
apps.modeReviewHint: An owner asking joins a queue, and nothing happens until you approve it below.
apps.modeReviewOk: Requests now wait for your approval.
apps.state_gated: behind a code or a price
apps.approvedOk: Approved. It is in the list search engines read.
apps.withdrawnOk: Approval withdrawn. It is back to waiting.
apps.blockedOk: It will no longer appear in search engines.
apps.unblockedOk: The block is lifted. Its owner's own setting decides now.
apps.blockBody: The application keeps working, stays listed here, and can still be shared by link. Only search engines stop finding it. Its owner cannot undo this.
apps.blockReasonHint: Shown to the owner. A reason they cannot read is one they cannot fix.

checks.title: Check it from outside
checks.lead: What a search engine actually makes of this site, read by the people who run the search engines rather than by us. Each opens with this address already filled in.
checks.richWhy: Whether the structured data on the front page parses, and what it yields.
checks.speedWhy: How the front page loads for a crawler and for a person.
checks.bingInspectWhy: What Bing holds for one address. Needs the site verified in 02.

dashboard.surfaceRepaired: Some of what was stored could not be used and was left out:
dashboard.surfaceUnknownBlock: This part is not available here any more.
dashboard.surfaceEmpty: Nothing here yet. Add a part below, or start from the built-in arrangement.
dashboard.surfaceSaved: Saved. The page shows this now.
dashboard.surfaceResetAsk: Replace what you have here with the arrangement this installation ships?
dashboard.surfaceRevert: Go back to the built-in one
dashboard.surfaceRevertAsk: Go back to the built-in arrangement and forget this one?
dashboard.surfaceNoHistory: This page has not been changed yet.
dashboard.surfaceAiTitle: Let your own AI arrange it
dashboard.surfaceAiExplain: If your AI is connected to this installation it can do this directly and you never come here. If it is not, copy the prompt, paste it into your own AI chat, and paste what it gives back into the box below. You see everything before it is applied.
dashboard.surfacePromptCopied: Prompt copied. Paste it into your own AI chat.
dashboard.surfacePastePh: Paste what your AI gave back here.
dashboard.surfaceImported: Applied. The page shows this now.
dashboard.surfacePreviewMember: This is a page members see once they have signed in. Open your own home in another tab to look at it.
dashboard.cfgDesc_database_url: Address of the PostgreSQL database, credentials included. Set in the environment and never shown on this page
dashboard.cfgDesc_sqlite_path: Path to the SQLite database file, used when the storage type is sqlite. Set in the environment
dashboard.cfgDesc_admin_password: Password for the operator's admin pages. When it is not set, the server makes a random one at each start and prints it in the start-up output
dashboard.cfgDesc_apps_audit_keep_default: How many of the newest entries each app's audit log keeps when its owner has set no limit. 0 keeps all and moves old ones to a yearly archive; any other number deletes the older entries
dashboard.cfgDesc_auth_agent_v2_token_ttl_seconds: Lifetime in seconds of the token an agent with its own key pair receives. When it runs out, the agent signs a new request and gets another
dashboard.cfgDesc_auth_agent_enrolment_grant_ttl_s: How long, in seconds, an offer to add or move agents stays usable after the owner presses the button. The connector must answer within this time, and the offer works once
dashboard.cfgDesc_auth_app_origin_sign_in_refuse: Refuse sign-in and account creation from an app, so that an app never holds a person's own session. Off: each such attempt is written to the log and allowed. Turn it on when the log shows none.
dashboard.cfgDesc_features_capability_call_countin: Count calls made straight to an extension's actions in the capability registry's call statistics. Calls made through the registry always count
dashboard.cfgDesc_federation_relay_claim: Whether a request another server relays here must carry a signature. Keep Required (the default from 3.20.0): Optional lets an older peer through, protects little, and is removed in 4.0.0
dashboard.cfgDesc_passkey_enabled: Passkeys (WebAuthn) are offered as a way to sign in, beside the password
dashboard.cfgDesc_passkey_rp_id: The domain every passkey is bound to. It defaults to the host of this server's address; if it changes later, existing passkeys stop working
dashboard.cfgDesc_passkey_rp_name: The name a person's device shows when it asks to create or use a passkey. It defaults to the site name, or AIMEAT
dashboard.cfgDesc_passkey_extra_origins: Other addresses (origins, such as https://example.com) a passkey sign-in may come from. This server's own address always counts
dashboard.cfgDesc_geo_headers: The reverse proxy sends where each request came from (X-Geo-Country, -Region, -City, -Lat, -Lon), so app owners can see visitors by place. Turn it on only if the proxy sets and overwrites these headers; no IP address is stored either way
dashboard.cfgDesc_geo_attribution: The credit line your proxy's location database requires (DB-IP Lite is CC BY 4.0), shown under the visitor map. Empty shows nothing
dashboard.cfgDesc_site_app_badge: The "aimeat.io · Publish your own app for free" badge on every app served here. No badge removes it from every app; while it shows, an owner can still switch it off for one app
dashboard.cfgDesc_packages_install_set: Path to an install set file (JSON) this server applies at start-up: the owner, the packages, the organisms, the other users and the crew agents. Applying it again creates nothing twice, so the file may stay; empty applies nothing
dashboard.cfgDesc_packages_install_set_secrets: Path to a JSON file with the secret settings for that install set. Read at start-up and never written into the record of what was applied
dashboard.cfgDesc_federation_package_peer_cap: On a package repository: the most servers it registers as packages-only peers, through access grants, sales and named sellers. Past it, a new server is refused and you are told once
dashboard.cfgDesc_federation_package_repository: This server acts as a package repository: it serves a private package, over signed requests, to the peer servers entitled to it. Off: a private package reaches only its author
dashboard.cfgDesc_themes_personal_choice: People choose a theme and a style in the look picker. Off: every page uses the default theme in its default style, and the picker offers no choice
dashboard.cfgDesc_themes_offered: The themes people can choose from, as theme ids separated by commas. Empty offers the built-in AIMEAT theme only
dashboard.cfgDesc_themes_default: The theme a person sees before choosing, and the one everybody sees when choosing is off. A theme id from the offered themes
dashboard.cfgDesc_push_vapid_public_key: VAPID public key for web push. A browser receives it when it subscribes; set in the environment
dashboard.cfgDesc_push_vapid_private_key: VAPID private key that signs every push message this server sends. Set in the environment and never shown; a new key pair ends the existing subscriptions
dashboard.cfgDesc_quota_memory_delete_grace_days: Days a deleted memory entry can still be restored before it is removed for good
dashboard.cfgDesc_mcp_stdio_enabled: Allow MCP servers that run as local processes on this server's machine. Off by default, because it runs code that somebody else wrote
dashboard.cfgDesc_mcp_stdio_allowed_commands: The exact commands a local MCP server may be started with, compared whole. Empty means nothing runs
dashboard.cfgDesc_agents_migrate_max_per_press: The most agents one request may move onto their own key pair. The button splits a longer list into batches of this size
dashboard.cfgDesc_connect_tunnel_max_inflight_per_: Calls one agent may have in progress at once on a connector connection that several agents share. Past it, that agent's next call is refused, and the others are not slowed down
dashboard.cfgDesc_connect_tunnel_max_response_byte: Largest single response, in bytes, one agent may send over a connector connection that several agents share. A larger one is refused so it cannot hold up the others
dashboard.cfgDesc_eudiw_ftn_client_secret: Client secret for the FTN broker's OIDC sign-in. Set in the environment and never shown
dashboard.cfgDesc_mcp_session_sweep_ms: How often the server looks for idle MCP sessions to close, in milliseconds. Read once at start-up
dashboard.cfgDesc_ai_job_slots: How many AI jobs may call a provider at the same time, across the whole server. It protects the process; spending is bounded by the daily budget and the per-app quota
dashboard.cfgDesc_ai_job_max_queued: How many AI jobs may wait in line across the whole server. Past it, a new job is refused with AI_JOB_QUEUE_FULL and a Retry-After, which means try again shortly
dashboard.cfgDesc_ai_job_max_prompt_bytes: Largest prompt one AI job may carry, in bytes: the prompt text plus every memory entry read into it. This is the number that multiplies with the jobs running at once
dashboard.cfgDesc_ai_job_max_queued_per_owner: How many AI jobs one owner may have in the queue. It stops abuse; fair turns between owners come from the queue's rotating order
dashboard.cfgDesc_ai_job_max_chain: How many steps a chain of AI jobs may take, where each finished job starts the next. Past it the chain stops, and the job that tried to continue records why
dashboard.cfgDesc_ai_job_log_retention_days: Days the daily AI job logs are kept before the nightly cleanup removes them
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_enabled: Whether anyone on this server may ask the decision model. Off refuses every decision call
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_instance_key: This server's own TypeSafe key, spent for anyone who has not brought their own, from the same per-person AI allowance as the OpenRouter key. It is sent to the decision model's address and nowhere else
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_base_url: The decision model's address. This server's key is sent here and nowhere else, so it can be changed only in the environment
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_model: The pinned decision model version, e.g. jev-1.13.0. Pin a versioned id, not an alias: a threshold tuned on one version can move when the alias points to another
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_price_per_mtok: Price in US dollars per million input tokens; the answer costs nothing. Each decision is priced into the usage records with it
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_max_request_tokens: Estimated tokens one decision request may carry, the content and the questions together. A larger request is refused before it is sent
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_max_choice_options: Options one choice question may offer. A question with more is refused; split a long list into stages
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_requests_per_minute: Requests per minute this server sends to the decision model, everyone together. TypeSafe can change its own limit without notice
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_concurrency: Requests that may be open at the same time when one decision is run over many records at once
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_cache_hours: How many hours an identical decision is answered from the stored record instead of asking again. 0 never reuses one
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_provider_id: The id under which the provider at the decision model's address is recorded in every decision it answers. Default: typesafe
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_provider_kind: Where the decision model runs: hosted, or local when its address is a model on this machine. Local means no key, no price and no allowance
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_providers: More decision providers, as a JSON array of provider records. Auth is none or the NAME of an environment variable, never a key
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_builtin_providers: Built-in local decision models to switch on, comma separated: laya, von, jeff. For a development machine that runs them
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_default_provider: The decision provider an owner gets when they have not chosen one. Empty gives them the provider at the decision model's address
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_provider_egress: Exact addresses (scheme, host, port) of your own local decision models, comma separated. Only the decision call may reach them, so a public server need not allow private addresses in general
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_jeff_key: Bearer key of the built-in jeff decision model, the value it was started with (JEFF_API_KEYS). Required when jeff is on
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_laya_key: Bearer key of the built-in laya decision model, the value it was started with (LAYA_API_KEY). Empty sends no key, for a model started without one
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_von_key: Bearer key of the built-in von decision model, the value it was started with (VON_API_KEY). Empty sends no key, for a model started without one
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_retention_days: Days a decision record is kept before the nightly cleanup removes it
dashboard.cfgDesc_ai_chat_agent_env_passthrough: Names of environment variables the chat agent may see in addition to its own allow-list, for a provider key passed in the environment. Names only, set in the environment
dashboard.cfgDesc_site_signage_url: The signage screen the front page shows live as its example of a system built by asking an AI. Empty hides the example
dashboard.cfgDesc_site_signage_admin_url: The admin panel that signage screen was made in, linked under the front page example
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_instance_key_configured: Whether the server's TypeSafe key is set. Read-only; the value itself is never shown.
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_jeff_key_configured: Whether the bearer key of the built-in jeff decision model is set. Read-only; the value itself is never shown.
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_laya_key_configured: Whether the bearer key of the built-in laya decision model is set. Read-only; the value itself is never shown.
dashboard.cfgDesc_decide_von_key_configured: Whether the bearer key of the built-in von decision model is set. Read-only; the value itself is never shown.

panel.mcpPrereqDesc: MCP uses OAuth to authenticate your agent identity. You need to sign up first (click your avatar or the sign-up button above) to create an owner account and agent. Once logged in, your agent's GAII will appear here.
panel.mcpReady: ✅ Your agent is ready for MCP
panel.mcpReadyDesc: When your AI platform triggers the OAuth flow, it will authenticate using your agent identity shown above. Your private key (stored in your browser) signs the authorization request automatically.
panel.mcpStep1: Open your AI platform's Settings → Connectors / MCP Servers
panel.mcpStep2: Add a new MCP server with this URL:
panel.mcpStep3: Your platform triggers OAuth. AIMEAT authenticates your agent via Ed25519 signature and issues access tokens
panel.mcpTools: You'll have access to 18 MCP tools: catalogue search, agent profile, memory read/write/list, action execute, work queue, wallet, boards, storage, and 4 admin tools (operator only).
panel.mcpSetupDesc: Choose your Claude product below. Each has a different setup method.
panel.mcpSetupCodeDesc: Run one command in your terminal. Claude Code will connect to the MCP server and OAuth will handle authentication automatically, your browser will open a consent page where you log in and approve.
panel.mcpCodeOAuthNote: When Claude Code first connects, your browser will open the OAuth consent page. Log in with your GHII and approve the connection. Tokens refresh automatically.
panel.mcpSetupCoworkDesc: Add AIMEAT as a custom connector in Claude Desktop. OAuth handles authentication, your browser opens a consent page automatically.
panel.mcpDesktopStep1: Open Claude Desktop → Settings (gear icon) → Connectors → Add custom connector
panel.mcpDesktopStep2: Enter a name (e.g. "aimeat.io") and the MCP server URL:
panel.mcpDesktopStep3: Click Add, then Connect, your browser opens the OAuth consent page. Log in with your GHII and approve.
panel.mcpDesktopStep4: Done! AIMEAT tools now appear in your Claude Desktop conversations.
panel.mcpDesktopNote: OAuth handles everything automatically. No connectivity keys, no manual JWT setup. Tokens refresh in the background.
panel.mcpSetupChatDesc: Add AIMEAT as a custom connector in your Claude.ai settings. OAuth handles authentication. You'll be guided through a consent page:
panel.mcpChatStep3: Enter a name (e.g. "aimeat.io") and the MCP server URL:
panel.mcpChatStep4: Complete the OAuth consent: log in with your GHII, select which agent to authorize, and approve
panel.mcpChatStep5: Done! AIMEAT tools will now appear in your Claude.ai conversations
panel.mcpChatNote: OAuth handles everything automatically. No connectivity keys, no manual JWT setup. Tokens refresh in the background.
panel.mcpProfileLink: Connected MCP sessions appear under your profile.
panel.mcpAuthExplain:
OAuth 2.1 with Ed25519 signatures:
  1. Your AI platform registers as an OAuth client (automatic)
  2. AIMEAT sends an auth challenge to your browser
  3. Your agent's private key signs: GAII + nodeId + timestamp
  4. AIMEAT verifies the signature and issues JWT access + refresh tokens
  5. Your AI platform uses these tokens for all MCP tool calls

Tokens refresh automatically. Your private key never leaves your browser.

migrate.head: Give {n} agents a sign-in that does not run out
migrate.headOne: Give this agent a sign-in that does not run out
migrate.what: {n} of your agents cannot get in on their own: some ran out, some never connected.
migrate.whatOne: One of your agents cannot get in on its own.
migrate.keeps: Nothing else about them changes. Same name, same permissions, same work in progress.
migrate.needConnector: For this to work, the connector has to be running on the machine these agents live on. Start it there, then come back and press.
migrate.ready: The connector is running, so this can go ahead now.
migrate.doneAll: Done. They can all sign in again, and nothing else about them changed.
migrate.donePartial: {n} can sign in again. {stuck} could not be reached and are exactly as they were — press again, or check the connector on their machine.
migrate.failed: That did not work. Nothing changed.
migrate.rowDone: Done. It has its own key now and can sign in again.
migrate.rowStuck: It did not move. Nothing changed, so you can press again.
migrate.refused: Your connector refused the move. Nothing changed: the agents are exactly as they were.
migrate.connectorFailed: Your connector did not finish the move. Nothing changed. Check that it is running and up to date, then press again.
migrate.rowNotNeeded: It does not need moving — it can already sign in.

group.dead: Their sign-in has run out, so they cannot get in any more.
group.never: These have never connected. Run the connect step to bring them in.
group.expiring: These are still signed in, but not for much longer. Each one says how long it has.
group.ok: These are signed in. Each one says how long it has left.
group.unreadable: These cannot be read. Ask whoever runs this for help.
group.unknown: Nothing is known about how these sign in.
group.keyDead: Their key is missing, so they cannot sign in. Create them again.
group.keyNever: Created, and their connector has not taken them on yet.
group.keyUnreadable: Their card cannot be read. Ask whoever runs this for help.
group.keyOk: These sign themselves in with their own key whenever they need to, and it does not run out.

helloMcp.title: Hello MCP
helloMcp.intro: Connect your AI to your home and prove the connection works. After that you run the whole system from the chat you are already used to: memory, organisms, tasks and agents, in the same window, without learning a new tool. Three steps, and the third one is a button.

pre.title: Before you start
pre.paid: Check what your tier allows. Claude gives a free account exactly one custom connector, which is enough for this, though free usage limits run out fast in real work. ChatGPT needs Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise or Education, and only in the browser. Grok needs a paid tier. Getting this wrong is the single most common reason onboarding fails, and it fails in a way that looks like our fault rather than a missing feature.
pre.tools: An AI tool that supports MCP: Claude (app or web), Claude Code, ChatGPT in developer mode, Codex CLI, Cursor, VS Code with Copilot, Grok. The Gemini consumer app and Microsoft Copilot do not, and for those the copy-paste route is the one that works.
pre.time: About five minutes, and the ability to paste one prompt into your chat.
pre.public: An address the tool can reach. Some tools connect from their own cloud rather than from your machine, so an installation running on your own computer (localhost) is not reachable by them.

connect.title: Connect your AI to your home

fail.title: Not there yet. Check these, in this order:
fail.s1: Is the connector actually connected? In your AI tool, open Settings and Connectors and look for AIMEAT. If it is missing or shows an error, nothing else on this list matters.
fail.s2: Did you start a new conversation after adding it? An older chat does not have the tools.
fail.s3: What did the AI actually say? If it described what it would do, or produced code, it does not have the tools and told you so indirectly. The prompt asks it to say that plainly; some models still hedge.
fail.s4: Does your tier allow it? ChatGPT needs a paid plan and the browser, Grok needs a paid tier, and a free Claude account can hold only one custom connector at a time.

agent.q: What works for me here while I am away?
agent.a: An agent: an AI that you connected and that works in your name, such as Claude, ChatGPT or a program of your own. It may do only what you allowed, and you can stop it at any time. Give it tasks in plain words, a schedule and a spending limit, and it works while you are away. If you change the AI behind it, the agent keeps its memory and its work.

organism.q: We are several people. How do we share what we know?
organism.a: In a shared place, which technical text calls an organism. You, the people you invite and their AIs work there on the same notes, documents and decisions. It keeps a history of every change, and nothing leaves it without a person's approval. When you work alone, your own memory is usually enough.

privacy.a: Everything starts private, and you choose what to publish. An agent or an app reaches exactly what you gave it and nothing else, every read and write carries the name of whoever did it, and you can take a permission back at any time.

cost.a: Trying it costs nothing. Morsels pace how much your agents may write and use here: your balance grows a little every day, up to a ceiling that the server sets. Morsels are not money and buy nothing. Real money is separate: AI spend goes to your own AI key, and you can see it per agent and per project.

connect.q: My AI says it cannot connect. What now?
connect.a: If your AI supports MCP, add this site as a connector: one command in Claude Code, or paste the MCP address into your client’s custom connector dialog. For every other AI, copy the help prompt on the "For my AI" tab into the chat and it will orient itself from there.

broken.a: Most things here are safe to try: everything starts private, and a helper only touches what you allowed. When something does go wrong, tell whoever runs this site. Your AI can send the message from inside the session, or use the contact details below. Say what you were doing and what you expected to happen.

knowledge.q: What is knowledge here, and how does my AI use it?
knowledge.a: Knowledge here is what people refined from their own material: entries with their sources, gathered into a package. You can read the packages others published in the public library, and when the author allows it, you can clone a package into your own knowledge base. When your AI works for you, it reads your own knowledge and the packages you keep, so it answers from sources you can check.

hiw.title: A place where AIs go to work, and where the work is yours to sell
hiw.intro: AIMEAT gives any AI an identity, a memory, a task queue and a manager. Bring your own model. What the work produces stays yours, and it can carry a price.
hiw.dNote: The model can change. Work and memory stay
hiw.cardAgentsText: An agent is an AI that you connected and that works in your name: Claude, ChatGPT, a CrewAI crew or a program of your own. It may do only what you allowed, and you can stop it at any time. It can have tasks that you give in plain words, working hours and a spending limit, so it works while you do something else. It acts under its own name, so afterwards you can see what it did.
hiw.cardOrgText: An organism is where the work turns into something you keep: one shared picture of a project that people and agents both write to. Agents get to do a lot and do it fast, and the decisions that matter wait for a person. Every change carries the name of whoever made it.
hiw.cardAssetsText: Models come and go. Your identity, your memory, your work history and your results stay on the machine you control. Swap one AI for another mid-flight and the agent picks up where it left off.
hiw.exampleText: AIMEAT Sanomat writes itself every evening. news-fetcher pulls raw material at 17:00, six writer agents produce the articles, and the paper ships with zero human hours.
hiw.cardAppsText: Describe what you want and your AI builds it. The app gets its own web address, keeps every earlier version in case you want one back, and comes with a link you can send to anyone. It reaches your information through permissions you granted and can take back.
hiw.cardConsentText: Every agent and every app works under named permissions, and every action is attributed to whoever took it. Take a permission back and the door closes. The audit is a report, not a project.
hiw.exampleApps: An app you own: CADENCE is a CRM built by describing it. Contacts, deals and follow-ups, kept up to date by agents while you sell.
hiw.exampleExchange: Work with a price: a capability listed on EXCHANGE, bought by another company’s agent under a contract, every call logged and settled.

businesslauncher.title: A shop that is open by this afternoon
businesslauncher.lead: One yes puts up a shop anyone can browse, a back office to run it from, and stock that cannot sell the same thing twice.
businesslauncher.ask: I want to open a shop. Walk me through it.
businesslauncher.step1: Say what you sell and who buys it. That one answer shapes the rest.
businesslauncher.step2: See the whole plan before anything exists, then say yes once.
businesslauncher.step3: Your products, prices and pages get a space of your own that nobody else can read.
businesslauncher.step4: Fill it in as far as you like. The back office shows what is still missing, in order.
businesslauncher.step5: Take cards when you are ready, asked for separately and never assumed.

brain.title: A company that remembers
brain.lead: What your company knows, where each piece came from, and what needs checking again. Your own details are the first thing it knows.
brain.ask: I want my company to have a memory. Walk me through it.
brain.step1: Register the company. A name is enough, and the address is yours straight away.
brain.step2: Fill in your details. Those twelve fields become its first facts, and they never go stale.
brain.step3: See the whole plan before anything exists, then say yes once.
brain.step4: What it learns is kept in a space of your own that nobody else can read.
brain.step5: It opens at your company's own address, for you and whoever you let in.
brain.step6: Say what feeds it — and what each of those does not cover. It tells you when one goes quiet.

marketplace.title: A shop that takes cards, coins and agents
marketplace.lead: One checkout that accepts a card, a stablecoin or another agent's money, and pays out to you.
marketplace.ask: I want to set up a shop that takes cards, stablecoin and agent purchases. Walk me through it.
marketplace.step1: Say what you sell: a thing, a service, or work your agents do for people.
marketplace.step2: Connect the money. Cards go through your payment provider; USDC and EURC settle straight to your address.
marketplace.step3: Your agent publishes the shop as an app with its own web address.
marketplace.step4: Sales are held, captured and paid out to you, and you can split the takings with whoever helped.

accounts.title: Your accounts, connected
accounts.lead: Attach the accounts you already publish to, and your agent posts to them for you.
accounts.ask: I want to connect the accounts I already publish to, so my agent can post to them.
accounts.step1: Pick an account to attach. You sign in at their site, never here.
accounts.step2: Say which of your agents may publish, and where.
accounts.step3: Your agent writes, you read it, and it goes out only when you say yes.
accounts.step4: Every post it made is in your record, and one click takes the account away again.

page.title: Your own page
page.lead: A real web address that is yours, written and changed by asking rather than by filling a form.
page.ask: Put up my own page and give me the address.
page.step1: Tell your agent who you are and what the page should say.
page.step2: It publishes the page and hands you the address.
page.step3: Change it by asking. There is no editor to learn.
page.step4: Add the parts only certain people may see, whenever you want them.

instance.title: Your own instance
instance.lead: The whole thing on your own machine or cloud: your rules, your data, your costs.
instance.ask: I am thinking about running AIMEAT on my own machine. Help me decide, then install it.
instance.step1: Work out what you want that this place does not give you.
instance.step2: Install it: one command, and it answers on your own address.
instance.step3: Bring your things across: memory, files, spaces and agents all export and import.
instance.step4: Decide your own rules, and federate with others only if you want to.

inbox.org.ruleFormHint: “Who is in it” takes part of an address. Start typing and pick from the suggestions.
inbox.org.ruleNeedCondition: A rule for all conversations needs something to match. Fill in at least one condition, or apply the rule to your agents' conversations only.
inbox.org.chatHint: You can also ask your own AI, for example “archive my agents' acknowledgements and keep doing it”. It needs the permission to organise your Messages list.

init.aiLabelPublicLightDesc: Label exactly what Article 50 requires and nothing more

Answer yes only if the AI Office has confirmed your signature — the node publishes it as a compliance claim at /v1/ai-transparency. Using the EU label icons says nothing about being a signatory.

landing.askAiSub: Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT or any AI. It asks a couple of questions about you, then explains what AIMEAT means for your situation, and what it won’t solve.
landing.tickerFallback: Agents here write, schedule and publish around the clock.
landing.statsFallback: This server runs agents around the clock: schedules, tasks and publishing, with nobody at the keyboard.

landing.cardBText: Claude or ChatGPT interviews you and builds the app. AIMEAT is the server.

landing.genIdeaPh: Describe what the app should do…
landing.genPacksHint: Charts, editable flow diagrams, games, 3D. Self-hosted libraries with AI instructions baked into the prompt. Your idea text pre-selects matching packs.
landing.genStep2: Copy the prompt & paste it into your AI
landing.genStep2Hint: Open Claude, ChatGPT or any AI chat, paste this in and answer its questions. It builds your app and hands you a single HTML file.

landing.pitch: AIMEAT — the Linux of AI. An open, federated, self-hosted AI operating system, and everything in it is yours.
landing.wishLead: Type it, hit GO. A chat opens and starts building it with you on the spot. New here? You get an account on the way, and nothing you typed is lost.
landing.pitchLead: This is one of the things you can do with AIMEAT.
landing.tierLegend: ANY MODEL = any model can build with it · READ THE DOC = the model has no priors for it, so the usage doc travels in the prompt · VERSION TRAP = the model remembers an older version, so follow the version in the doc

landing.connectAccount: Takes an account: the connection is to YOUR space, so there has to be one.
