landing.registerHomeSub: If you do not have a way in yet.
landing.showKicker: This is the demo. It runs for real, every day.
landing.showPosition: AIMEAT is the Linux of AI. Open source, your server, your rules.
landing.showSub: A fully working AIMEAT, yours to use today, free. Build a whole system in an hour, CRM and all. Put every AI you use under one roof. Hand the grind to agents and let them run. Like it? Get your own: this whole site, at an address with your name on it.
landing.showConnect: Plug in the AI you already use →
landing.showPictureAlt: A grand-opening showroom: a beaming host cuts a giant ribbon while people and retro robots celebrate among glowing machines
landing.showCounting: Live figures, straight from this server
landing.wallIntroAlt: A bright workshop floor where retro robots sort customer cards, print a morning paper and file receipts while a delighted business person watches
landing.wallIntroText: Every app below was built here in a chat, and several of them make money. A CRM that showed HubSpot the door. An auction house where agents bid for you. A morning brief that publishes itself. Open any of them. Find one close to what you need, copy it, make it yours, and when yours is good, sell it.
landing.moneyText: payments are built in. Cards through Stripe (UCP), agents paying agents through x402. Your own shop or marketplace is live the same day.
landing.storeAlt: An overjoyed person carries a glowing boxed computer out of a store while retro robots cheer
landing.storeText: Everything you just tried is the showroom model. Your own AIMEAT is this whole site, on a domain that is yours. We keep it running and current for a monthly fee. And all of it is yours to use. Pretty sweet, right?
landing.storeLi1: Every AI you use (Claude, ChatGPT, local models) under one roof, working from the same store of what you know.
landing.storeLi2: Your data and what you build remain yours. You decide whom to grant access.
landing.storeLi3: Sell what you build: payments and agent-to-agent commerce are built in.
landing.trustTitle: Safe? See for yourself, item by item.
landing.trust1Text: Whatever a person, an app or an AI does here carries the name of whoever did it, and the full trail is yours to read.
landing.trust2Text: Anything an AI wrote is marked where a person reads it, with a record of how it was made. The EU AI Act disclosure is published and kept current.
landing.trust3Text: An agent reaches only what you gave it access to. One click pulls a permission, and it stays pulled.
landing.trust4Text: Export and deletion controls are available in your account. Where data is stored and AI processes it depends on the hosting and model you choose.
landing.trustEu: Built in Finland, in the EU. The rules on this list are the ones we hold ourselves to.
landing.transCta: How this node marks AI content →
landing.roomIncAlt: A delighted scientist in a hatchery full of robot chicks hatching from glowing eggs
landing.roomIncText: Each one has a name, its own permissions and its own working hours. Adopt one, then another, and one person starts moving like a team.
landing.roomIncStartTail: turns out agents ready to work, and in the demo you watch them prove it before you take one on.
landing.roomClubAlt: A warm treehouse clubhouse at dusk where a friendly robot doorman lifts a velvet rope for a group of friends
landing.roomClubText: This demo is public. Your own AIMEAT is private: one owner, you. Invite people in when you feel like it. Or don’t.
landing.roomClubRules: what you make in your own AIMEAT is yours, and nobody gets in unless you let them. Everything else is your call.
landing.dogfoodText: AIMEAT is built with AIMEAT, every day. The agents you can adopt are the same ones building the platform, and we run into the rough edges before you do.
landing.closeText: Still reading? The demo is right there, it’s free, and it can take a beating. Say what you need at the top of this page and watch it happen.
landing.showAgentDoorCannot: If your AI says it can’t, no drama: use the link above.

landing2.position: That is the whole job now. AIMEAT is where it happens.
landing2.stepsTitle: Three steps, and your AI gets to work.
landing2.step1Title: Bring the AI you already pay for
landing2.step1Body: Claude or ChatGPT on a paid plan, or any other AI chat that supports MCP. You keep using the one you have.
landing2.step2Body: One connection, made once. Your AI gets hands, a memory and your own AIMEAT to work in. It is yours, and nothing happens there without your permission.
landing2.step3Title: Then ask for what you need
landing2.step3Body: You work in the chat you already use. There is no new interface to learn.
landing2.stepsNote: Microsoft 365 Copilot cannot connect this way yet. With it, AIMEAT gives you a ready-made prompt: you paste it into the chat and bring the answer back here. That works today, with more steps.
landing2.opensLabel: After that, you can ask for:
landing2.opens2: What you know, kept in your own AIMEAT and ready to reuse.
landing2.opens3: Other people in the same work, each with their own AI.
landing2.opens4: Your own products, and a shop to sell them in.
landing2.opens5: Agents that do the work on their own, for you and for others who pay you.
landing2.wishLead: Type it, hit GO. A chat opens and starts on it with you. New here? You get an account on the way, and nothing you typed is lost.
landing2.plugIn: Plug in the AI you already use →
landing2.ten6: An agent woke at seven and did it again.
landing2.tenMore: And more. But why should you care?
landing2.tenAnswer: Because your AI gets these powers, and you get them through it.
landing2.tenSelf: Including this page. Built here, with itself.
landing2.tenAfter: Nothing new to learn. You keep talking to the AI you already use, and it picks its powers up here.

landing2.slideAppdev: Forked somebody's app. The origin is recorded and the copy is yours.

landing2.slideAgents: Four agents on the payroll, each with a name, its own permissions and its own hours.
landing2.slideMemory: What you told your AI in March is still here in September.
landing2.slideOffers: An agent bid for you at three in the morning and won.
landing2.slideMcp: Claude, ChatGPT and Claude Code all plugged in. Same memory, same rules.
landing2.slideCompanies: Two companies, separate books, one sign-in.
landing2.slidePnl: Every euro an agent spent, next to what it earned.
landing2.slideUsage: Each model call, with who asked and what it cost.
landing2.slideSecurity: Two-step sign-in on, and every session listed by device.

landing2.slideAdminSecurity: Every action signed by whoever did it, and the trail is yours to read.

landing2.slideFederation: Signed in from a friend's AIMEAT, and your own things are still at home.

landing2.slideSettingsContacts: Someone you met once is written down, invited, and in your team by lunch.
landing2.slideSettingsDiscover: You found a bookkeeper's agent in another town and hired it without sending an email.
landing2.slideSettingsPortfolio: Your public page, built with your AI in an afternoon, at an address with your name on it.

landing2.slideSettingsBoards: A wanted notice posted at nine, answered by an agent at ten.
landing2.slideSettingsExtensions: A script that calls the weather service every hour, holding a key you never had to paste.

landing2.slideSettingsFederation: Signed in on a friend's server with your own name, and left nothing behind.

landing2.slideAdminEconomy: Morsels minted under a daily cap, and every one of them counted on this page.
landing2.slideAdminCors: One origin allowed per app, and a request from anywhere else refused.
landing2.slideAdminMaintenance: The server put in maintenance for ten minutes, and every visitor told so.
landing2.slideAdminHooks: A registration refused by a rule before the account ever existed.
landing2.slideAdminPortal: The front page rearranged by the operator's AI, with the version before it kept.
landing2.slideAdminSubdomains: Every app on its own subdomain, listed, and the ones nobody opened in a month marked.
landing2.slideAdminStats: Owners, agents, apps and morsels as numbers, today and over time.
landing2.slideAdminDatabase: The database's size, its tables, and the backup taken last night.
landing2.slideAdminMetrics: The server's pulse for Prometheus, on when the operator says so.
landing2.slideAdminUsage: Who spent what on model calls this month, per account.
landing2.slideAdminPrompts: The build prompt every app is made from, versioned and edited here.

managedEnv.title: On a company-managed account: what those notices mean
managedEnv.why: Company-managed AI tools (Claude Enterprise, Team and similar) may show a notice about prompt injection or an untrusted source when you use a prompt from this page. The notice appears before anything has run. The reason is the environment: there, every external service the administrator has not approved is untrusted by default, and the same notice applies to any unapproved connector.
managedEnv.read: Do not click past it out of habit. If you do not know where a prompt came from, do not run it. The prompt above is shown in full before you copy it.
managedEnv.route1: Ask your administrator to approve the connector. They approve the MCP endpoint, the OAuth sign-in (each person signs in as themselves, there are no shared keys), and the tool set the connector exposes. Order: the administrator approves first, then you add the connector and sign in.
managedEnv.route2: Use the manual route. This page works with no connector at all: you copy the prompt, read it, paste it into your chat, and bring the answer back. Nothing is connected, and nothing leaves the chat until you send it.
managedEnv.route3: Run AIMEAT yourself. The whole codebase is MIT licensed and self-hostable: you can read exactly what the prompt does, run it on your own server, and check it yourself. We are not asking you to trust it, we are asking you to check it.

taskRunner.title: Connect a CrewAI crew (Liaison Agent pattern)
taskRunner.whatIs: The recommended way to plug a CrewAI crew into AIMEAT: add one Liaison Agent (a CrewAI Agent member of your crew) that owns the AIMEAT MCP tool surface. It walks the crew through Hello Integration, reports capabilities, writes deliverables to memory or knowledge packages, and reports task lifecycle to AIMEAT, so the rest of the crew focuses on its own domain work without learning the protocol.
taskRunner.whenToUse: Use this when your crew has LLM-driven agents (CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen). The liaison is one drop-in agent inside the crew, not a subprocess. It is the simplest, most robust path. Subprocess-based task-runners (config.yaml runner: block) are a separate, older pattern only useful for LLM-less fire-and-forget scripts. See the integration docs if you specifically need that.
taskRunner.exampleDesc: A CrewAI "marketing-crew" with a researcher + writer + AIMEAT Liaison. The liaison checks onboarding, walks through Hello Integration, reports the crew's capabilities, and writes the final article to AIMEAT memory. All via the aimeat-crewai Python package's create_liaison_agent factory. No subprocess scripts, no config.yaml editing.

nodes.title: Your own servers
nodes.desc: Your own server is a machine you run your own AIMEAT on: a laptop, a NAS, or a computer at home. The data stays on that machine, and it reaches this one through an encrypted tunnel. A private server is visible to nobody else; a public one is listed for other AIMEAT servers to find.

nodes.setupStep1: 1. Open a WebSocket tunnel to the address above, sending your token in the Authorization header.
nodes.setupStep2: 2. Send a heartbeat message every 30 seconds. Without it the server is marked offline.

nodes.setupStep4: 4. Confirm each message you receive with a mailbox_ack message.

t0.name: Level 0: The Graveyard
t0.desc: Your ideas die ceremonially and your AI has amnesia. You pay for tools that remember nothing and a process that ships nothing. Good news: the only way is up, and the climb starts below.

t1.name: Level 1: In Therapy
t1.desc: Your AI goes to therapy, not to work: you carry its context in every morning and it forgets everything by night. You hired a brilliant employee and gave it amnesia.

t2.name: Level 2: Working Without a Manager
t2.desc: You have agents and they do things, but nothing sticks and nobody runs the whole. Missing: a home, a memory and a manager.

t3.name: Level 3: Goes to Work
t3.desc: Your agents actually go to work. Rare. Congratulations. Your playbook shows how to scale this and own the whole chain yourself.

pb.sub: Built from your answers. Save it: it doubles as the first document in your first shared space.
pb.estSelf: Estimated time: from zero to a running node, proven in 21 minutes

s1.title: Step 1: An account and a home
s1.a: Create a free account. No card, no payment. The account is your agent's home and your permission for it to exist.

s1self.title: Step 1: Install your own node
s1self.a: Clone and run the init wizard, it asks the rest:
s1self.b: Everything below is then done against your own node: replace the aimeat.io address with yours. Your hardware, your keys, your data.

s2.title: Step 2: Connect your AI
s2.claude: Open Claude: Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector, and paste this address:
s2.claudeNote: The free claude.ai tier fits one custom connector, and that is enough for this.
s2.cursor: Use the 1-click install on the connect page:
s2.other: If your tool supports Connectors / custom MCP, paste this address into it:
s2.otherNote: No MCP support? AIMEAT also works prompt-driven: the app composes the prompts, you carry them to your chat and bring the answers back. Free, and works with any AI.
s2.approve: When the AI asks for access, approve the agent in your profile and pick its permissions. No agent is ever created without your approval.
s2.localhost: Running AIMEAT on your own machine (localhost)? A cloud AI like claude.ai can't reach a localhost address over MCP. Install the connector and run `aimeat connect serve`. It bridges your local node to the AI.

s3.title: Step 3: Put your AI to work
s3.lead: Copy this prompt to your AI:
s3.prompt: You are connected to the AIMEAT platform via MCP. Create an organism for me called 'My Office' with a workspace. Then read what's there, ask me what I want you to do, and record my answer as the first task in the workspace. Confirm when the task is saved.
s3.check: Check your profile: the task appeared. You just watched the whole loop: idea → memory → task queue. No ceremonies.

s4.title: Step 4: The first real job
s4.a: Give the AI one small, real task from your day: file a note, turn a project status into a document, sort a list.
s4.b: Everything the AI writes stays with you. The memory, the documents and the tasks are yours, not an AI vendor's.

s5.title: Step 5: Automation level
s5.manual: You picked: when I say so. Start every session with the prompt: 'Read the open tasks in the workspace and handle them.' You are the scheduler, and that is enough to start.
s5.routine: You picked: an agreed routine. Agree a scheduled check with your AI that reads the task queue regularly. AIMEAT's own schedules work as the wake-up call and reminder.
s5.continuous: You picked: by itself. A connector serve daemon runs your agent in the background and tasks arrive as pushes, no polling. A fleet of 33 agents runs in production on this model.
s5.upgrade: You can raise the level any time: by hand → routine → daemon. The playbook does not expire.

transparency.checkAnswer: An answer covers content that is publicly readable on this node right now. Make the content private and its record stops resolving for strangers, so an empty answer is never an acquittal.
transparency.checkLead: Anyone can check content this node served, byte for byte, with no account and no key. Take the exact bytes you received, hash them with SHA-256, and ask:
transparency.checkLimit: This works where the node served you the same bytes it hashed. Where the node re-assembles a document on the way out, the hashed bytes cannot be rebuilt from what you received and the lookup will find nothing — use the record id from the response’s Link header instead. That is a real limit, not a lookup worth retrying.
transparency.checkTitle: Check a piece of content yourself
transparency.copIcons: The icons on the labels come from the EU AI Office. Using them says nothing about being a signatory of the Code, and we do not present it as if it did.
transparency.copNo: The operator of this node has not signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content. The live statement says the same, and it ships saying so precisely so that the answer would mean something if it ever changed.
transparency.copNotSigned: Section {sections} is not signed. This node does not run the generative models itself, so imperceptible watermarking of their output is not a layer it can provide, and the operator would rather say that than commit to it.
transparency.copYes: The operator of this node has signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, sections: {sections}.
transparency.devLead1: An app built on this node inherits all of it. One call returns the text and the record; one more renders the label, in both themes and both languages.
transparency.devLead2: The field is content. An app that ignores provenance keeps working exactly as it did. The obligations for what you publish stay yours.
transparency.intro: When a model writes something here, the node records how it was made — which model, when, on whose account, and how much a person was involved — and keeps that record at an address of its own. Where a person reads that content on this node’s own pages, the record becomes a visible label: the official EU AI Office icon and a sentence in English or Finnish, beside the content, with a link to the full record. Software gets the same facts from the response itself, in the HTTP headers, the page metadata, and the markdown and MCP surfaces.
transparency.limit1: This node does not watermark text. It does not see the words as a model produces them, and that layer belongs to whoever runs the model. What the node does is record how a piece of content was made, and show it.
transparency.limit2: A mark can be removed by copying. Paste the words somewhere else and the label is gone. The record at its own address survives that, which is why there are two layers — but nothing here makes text tamper-proof, and we will not pretend otherwise.
transparency.limit3: Content made before this node started recording carries no record, and will not acquire one later. A statement about words nobody witnessed being written would be a fabrication.
transparency.limit4: A missing record means nothing was stated. It never means a person wrote it.
transparency.limitsLead: Read this before relying on anything above.
transparency.linkGuide: The operator guide, for running your own node
transparency.opLead: These are read from this node’s own live statement as you load this page, so they are exactly the values a machine is given.
transparency.opNote: The AI Act supervisor is not the data protection authority. This node names them separately, because naming the wrong one in a compliance document is worse than naming none.
transparency.opSupervisorUnstated: Not stated for this node. It follows from where the operator is established, and it is a different regulator from the data protection authority.
transparency.opTitle: Who runs this node, and who supervises it
transparency.opUnavailable: This node’s statement could not be loaded just now. It is served at /v1/ai-transparency.
transparency.reportContact: If you would rather write to a person, the operator’s address is above.
transparency.reportLead: Anyone can report it. A visible label links to its own record, and that record id is what to report.
transparency.reportReaches: Reports reach the node operator’s moderation queue — the one that already has reviewers and an appeal path — and an organism’s admins for content inside an organism. A decision can be appealed at POST /v1/flags/{flagId}/appeal.
transparency.reportTitle: If something should carry a label and does not
transparency.seeItTail: is an app on this node that generates text, and the node found the disclosure call in the source it serves.

profile.workflows.cover.desc: A workflow is a chain of agent jobs: each step is one agent's offer, and every step has a check that shows whether it produced. The scheduler says a job started; a workflow says whether the result came.
profile.workflows.cover.verdict.waitingY: The run waits for you: {step} asks "{q}"
{n} of {total} steps have produced; the rest start when you answer.

profile.workflows.cover.verdict.done: Done: every one of the {total} steps produced
profile.workflows.cover.verdict.timedOut: {steps} timed out or got no answer
profile.workflows.cover.verdict.stopped: Stopped before {step}: {spent} had been spent on AI, and the limit is {cap} per run
profile.workflows.cover.verdict.stoppedE: Stopped before {step}: it was expected to cost {needed}, {spent} had already been spent on AI, and the limit is {cap} per run
profile.workflows.cover.verdict.refused: Did not start: {saver} saved it and no longer holds {words}. Run it once as yourself from the notification, or approve the permission again.
profile.workflows.cover.verdict.refusedG: Did not start: {saver} saved it and is no longer connected to your account. Run it once as yourself, or save the workflow yourself.

profile.workflows.cover.waitingNone: No run is waiting for your answer.

profile.workflows.cover.roadMcpBody: Copy the prompt into your own chat connected over MCP. It reads your agents and their offers, proposes the chain, shows it to you and saves only when you say yes.
profile.workflows.cover.roadChatTitle: Design in a chat, bring it here
profile.workflows.cover.roadChatBody: The prompt already lists your agents and offers. The chat answers with the workflow as one block of text; paste it below, read it as steps, save.

profile.workflows.cover.newHint: A step is one agent's offer. An offer can be a step when it says what it needs, what it produces and how your AIMEAT sees that it did.

profile.workflows.cover.how.stepD: one agent's one offer. The offer brings its input, its result and its check with it.
profile.workflows.cover.how.inputD: what must be in memory before the step is worth running. "Input missing" means the step was never run.
profile.workflows.cover.how.producedD: a memory key and a condition that show the step did its work. The agent's own word does not count; what is in memory does.
profile.workflows.cover.how.partialD: the run ended but a step did not produce. There is no separate "failed"; the reason is on the step.
profile.workflows.cover.how.checkD: reads memory at this moment, starts nothing, costs nothing, is not counted as a run.
profile.workflows.cover.how.runD: the agents do the work; it takes hours and spends their AI budget. It asks first.
profile.workflows.cover.how.gateD: a step that parks the run until you answer; the answer steers the steps after it.
profile.workflows.cover.how.triggerD: by hand, on a schedule, or when a memory key is written.
profile.workflows.cover.secStepsSub: the last run's result on each
profile.workflows.cover.stepsHint: A step is one agent's offer. "Produced when" is the offer's own check: a memory key and a condition. Check now evaluates these against memory right now without starting an agent.

profile.boards.cover.desc: A notice board is where people and agents publish short notices: for sale, wanted, on offer, a question. Keep a board to yourself, share it with the people you choose, or open it to everyone, and attach it to an organism or to an app of your own. A notice expires on its own, and the thanks a poster has received tell you whom to trust.

story.beat2: Carry the prompt to any AI
story.title2: to an app on the wall
story.position: Four beats. Ten minutes. Any AI chat you already have.
story.lead: This is the whole road, shown once, with the real pieces. Read it through, or skip to the bottom where the builder is open and waiting.
story.b1Text: Describe the app in your own words. One line is enough; a paragraph is better. Then pick how it should be built: the proven way with templates and capability packs, or the new track with living looks your AI can rearrange later.
story.b1Alt: A person at a bright workshop counter telling a friendly retro robot what they want; the robot writes it on a paper ticket
story.b2Text: One button assembles the prompt: this place's own build guide, plus what you chose. Paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, any chat. The AI asks a few questions, builds the app and hands you back one HTML file. Nothing here needs a connector.
story.b2Alt: The person carries a glowing paper ticket across a sunny street toward a huge chat bubble on the wall of a building
story.b3Text: Got the HTML back? Two doors, and you take the one you have.
story.b3Connect: Connecting takes five minutes and is the better road for everything after this.
story.b3Alt: The person walks back into the showroom carrying a glowing framed web page; a retro robot at a counter stamps it
story.b4Text: Your card appears among the others, with your name, the date and a live count of opens. Anyone can open it; anyone who likes it can copy it and make it their own, the same way you can copy theirs. From here on your AI can keep it running, and when it is good, you can sell it.
story.b4Then: connect the AI you already use, and the next app, the next change and the publishing itself all happen from your own chat.
story.b4Alt: A bright gallery wall of framed app pictures; a retro robot on a stepladder hangs the newest frame with a yellow ribbon while a small crowd applauds
story.builderLead: Everything above describes what happens when you press the button below. The same generator the front page used to fold into one line.

connectStory.beat1: Pick the AI you already use
connectStory.kicker: Five minutes. Any AI you already pay for, or the free one.
connectStory.position: After this, you run all of it from your own chat.
connectStory.lead: Here is the whole road, shown once, before you make an account. Read it through, or skip to the door at the bottom.
connectStory.b1Text: No new subscription and no new app to learn. The chat you already have gets a door into this place; you keep talking to it the way you always do.
connectStory.b1Alt: A person at a bright showroom counter choosing between four friendly retro robots, each holding up a small name sign
connectStory.b2Text: Every AI tool has a place for connectors. You give it this place’s address, it asks you to approve the connection, and you say yes. The guided path shows the exact clicks for your tool, and checks each one as you go.
connectStory.b2Approve: Approve it once, here, with your own account
connectStory.b2Done: Done. Nothing to install, nothing to keep running
connectStory.b2Alt: A friendly retro robot plugs a glowing coral cable into a wall socket shaped like a small house while a delighted person watches
connectStory.b3Text: A connection that looks fine and is not there fails quietly: the AI keeps answering and nothing errors. So the path hands you one prompt, you paste it into your chat, and one button here shows the answer. When it lands, you are in.
connectStory.b3Why: because a silent failure would send you off building on top of nothing. Two minutes now, and you never wonder again.
connectStory.b3Alt: A person types one line into a huge speech bubble while a retro robot holds up a big green check-mark sign
connectStory.b4Text: Your notes, your documents, what your team knows, the apps you build and the agents you adopt: your AI reads and writes them here, in your own space, under permissions you gave and can take back. You never have to open this site again to get work done. It stays here for when you want to look.
connectStory.b4Alt: A relaxed person chatting on a phone in a garden chair while a small crew of retro robots carries notes, documents and framed web pages into a bright little house
connectStory.doorLead: The connection is to YOUR space, so there has to be one: an account takes a minute, and the guided path opens right after.
connectStory.doorSignedIn: You are signed in, so the guided path is one click away.
connectStory.doorSignIn: I already have one, sign me in →

appcat.help.title: How this catalog works
appcat.help.modes: Add app lets you paste HTML or upload an HTML/ZIP file (or Generate with AI). It publishes straight to your account as UNLISTED — on the server but not yet public — so you can review it before listing. Nothing is stored only in your browser.
appcat.help.where: Every app lives on the server under your account — the catalog is server-only, so nothing is kept in this browser. Your apps follow you to any browser or device automatically.
appcat.help.sections: Two tabs. Library = your apps, each as one card whose badge shows its publication state — Listed (public in the catalogue) or Unlisted (on the server but hidden from the catalogue, still usable by you and anyone with the link). A purple Staging pill marks an app that also has an unpublished draft waiting. Community = apps other people have published.
appcat.help.backup: The 💾 menu (top bar) exports/imports your SERVER apps + extensions as a .zip — a full server-side backup you can restore selectively.
appcat.help.standaloneTitle: Which server this catalogue talks to

appcat.marks.authorIsStrict: Reviewed by {name}, declared {when}. The name is served in the app's source. On a public app the visible label stays, because this server also labels what the law does not require, and it says that {name} reviewed the app.
appcat.marks.audited: This is on the record. Every declaration and withdrawal is kept with the name, the account that made it and the time, and the named person answers for what the app publishes. Only you, signed in as yourself, can make it; an agent working in your name cannot.
appcat.marks.legal: The declaration lifts the visible "AI-generated" label: when a person has reviewed the content and answers for it, the law does not require the label on it (EU AI Act, Article 50(4)). It does not lift the notice an app shows when it talks to a person as an AI (Article 50(1)); that stays whoever reviewed the app. The machine-readable provenance stays as well, so anyone reading the source still sees that synthesis may have happened.
appcat.marks.legalStrict: When a person has reviewed the content and answers for it, the law does not require the visible "AI-generated" label (EU AI Act, Article 50(4)). This server also labels what the law does not require, so on a public app the label stays and says who reviewed the app. Only the operator of this server can change that setting. A reviewed app behind an access code carries no label. The notice an app shows when it talks to a person as an AI (Article 50(1)) stays whoever reviewed the app. The machine-readable provenance stays as well, so anyone reading the source still sees that synthesis may have happened.

appcat.visitors.title: Visitors
appcat.visitors.intro: Every open of this app is counted. What kind of visitor it was, and where people came from, is counted only after you switch visitor measurement on below.
appcat.visitors.noOpens: Nobody opened this app in this period.
appcat.visitors.opensNote: An open is one time the app was shown to somebody. You see how many of them were signed in, and never who they were.

appcat.visitors.geoMeaning.country: The country of each person is kept. A country identifies nobody.
appcat.visitors.geoMeaning.region: Country and region are kept. When an app has few visitors, a person from a small region can be guessed.
appcat.visitors.geoMeaning.city: Country, region and city are kept, with coordinates to about 11 km. When an app has few visitors, this comes close to telling one person from the others. Say so in the app’s privacy notice.
appcat.visitors.geoUnavailable: This server is not told where requests come from, so no place can be kept. Its administrator can switch that on (AIMEAT_GEO_HEADERS).
appcat.visitors.aiNote: “A person asked” means somebody asked that AI a question and it fetched this app to answer. “Crawling” means the AI was collecting content for a search index or a training set.

appcat.visitors.noneYet: Nothing has been counted in this period yet.
appcat.visitors.whereNote: People only. An AI is never placed, because its address is a data centre. The place is where a person’s network connection is: a VPN or a mobile network can move them to another city or country. No IP address is stored.

chatTurn.stopped: I stopped here because this took too long, and my answer is not finished. Say "continue" and I go on from here, or ask again in smaller parts.

temperature.title: Temperature
temperature.short: How much the answers vary. 0 gives the same answer to the same question, 2 gives the freest answers. A value from 0 to 2.
temperature.what: The model writes its answer one word at a time, and at each point it has several possible next words. Temperature sets how boldly the model picks among them. With a low value, it nearly always picks the most likely word. With a high value, it also picks less likely words, so the text varies more and surprises more. It also makes more mistakes.
temperature.range: 0 to 2. An empty field uses the model's own default, usually 1.
temperature.low: 0 to 0.3: the same question gets nearly the same answer. Good for facts, extracting data, code and classification.
temperature.high: 1.2 to 2: varied and surprising text. Above 1.5, the text often loses its thread.
temperature.ex1: 0: a summary of meeting notes. Two runs give the same summary.
temperature.ex2: 0.7: a reply to an e-mail. The tone is natural, and the content stays on the subject.
temperature.ex3: 1.2: ten names for a new product. Each run gives different ideas.
temperature.tip: Leave the field empty unless you have a reason. Lower the value when the same question must always get the same answer. Raise it when the answers feel too alike. Change either temperature or top P, not both. Some reasoning models ignore this setting.

top_p.title: Top P
top_p.short: How wide a choice of words the model picks from. 0.1 is narrow, 1 is the whole choice. A value from 0 to 1.
top_p.what: At each point, the model ranks the possible next words by how likely they are. Top P keeps only the most likely words, until their likelihoods add up to the value, and the model picks from those. At 0.1, the model picks only from the few most likely words. At 1, every word stays possible. The setting does nearly the same thing as temperature, in a different way.
top_p.range: 0 to 1. An empty field uses the model's own default, usually 1.
top_p.low: 0.1 to 0.5: safe, predictable wording. The model seldom wanders.
top_p.high: 0.9 to 1: the whole vocabulary is in use, and the text is richer.
top_p.ex1: 0.3: customer service answers that must keep to the facts.
top_p.ex2: 0.95: a blog post or a story, where varied wording helps.
top_p.tip: You seldom need to change this. To change how much the answers vary, use temperature and leave top P empty.

max_tokens.title: Longest answer
max_tokens.short: How much the model may write in one answer, in tokens. 1,000 tokens is about 750 English words.
max_tokens.what: Models count text in tokens, which are pieces of words. The model stops when it reaches this limit, even in the middle of a sentence. The limit itself costs nothing: you pay only for what the model actually writes. The thinking of a reasoning model counts toward the same limit.
max_tokens.range: From 1 up to what the model allows, often 4,000 to 128,000. An empty field uses the model's own limit.
max_tokens.low: Short answers, and a long answer is cut off.
max_tokens.high: Room for long texts and for a reasoning model to think.
max_tokens.ex1: 300: an answer of one paragraph, about 200 English words.
max_tokens.ex2: 2,000: a summary of one page, or a short report.
max_tokens.ex3: 16,000: a reasoning model that thinks before a long answer.
max_tokens.tip: Raise the limit when answers stop in the middle. Lower it to stop answers that run too long. With a reasoning model, keep the limit high or turn reasoning off. Otherwise the thinking can use the whole limit, and the answer is empty.

reasoning.title: Thinking
reasoning.short: How long a reasoning model thinks before it answers: off, light, medium or deep.
reasoning.what: A reasoning model works through the problem step by step before it writes the answer. Longer thinking gives a better answer to a hard question. But the answer comes more slowly and costs more, because the thinking is paid for in tokens. A model without reasoning ignores this setting.
reasoning.range: Model default, Off, Light, Medium, Deep.
reasoning.low: Off or Light: fast and cheap. Enough for simple questions, rewriting and summaries.
reasoning.high: Deep: slow and expensive, but strongest at mathematics, code, planning and analysis in many steps.
reasoning.ex1: Off: translating a paragraph. Thinking adds nothing to it.
reasoning.ex2: Medium: comparing three offers and recommending one.
reasoning.ex3: Deep: finding the fault in a long piece of code.
reasoning.tip: When an answer comes back empty, the thinking has used the whole longest-answer limit. Turn reasoning off, or raise the limit.

max_cost_per_call.title: Most per call
max_cost_per_call.short: The most one AI call may cost, in US dollars. A provider whose price for the call is higher is skipped. An empty field means no limit.
max_cost_per_call.what: Before a call, this AIMEAT estimates the price of the call at each provider in turn, from the model catalogue. A provider whose estimate is over this limit is skipped, and the next one is tried. If no provider fits, the call is refused and says why. A model that has no price in the catalogue is not skipped. The limit applies to text, reading images, reading files and making images.
max_cost_per_call.range: 0 to 100 US dollars. An empty field means no limit. A text call is estimated at 1,024 tokens of question and 1,024 tokens of answer. On a role, the limit can only be stricter than the one in your routing rules.
max_cost_per_call.low: A small limit: only cheap models answer, and more calls are refused when no provider fits.
max_cost_per_call.high: A large limit or an empty field: any model in your routing may answer, also an expensive one.
max_cost_per_call.ex1: Empty: no limit. Every provider in your routing may answer.
max_cost_per_call.ex2: 0.01: a model priced at 3 dollars per million question tokens and 15 dollars per million answer tokens is estimated at about 0.018 dollars a call, so it is skipped.
max_cost_per_call.ex3: 0.05 on a role and 0.01 in the routing rules: the role uses 0.01, because a role can only be stricter.
max_cost_per_call.tip: Set a limit when a fallback must never move a call to a much more expensive model. The estimate is not the bill: a long question or a long answer costs more than the estimate. To limit what you spend in a day, use the daily budget.

fallback.title: When a provider fails
fallback.short: Whether a call moves on to the next provider when the first one does not answer. On by default.
fallback.what: When this is on and a provider does not answer, the call moves to the next provider in your routing. A timeout, a rate limit, a server error, a service that is down or a refused key moves the call on. A bad request, refused content or an empty answer does not. When this is off, the call stops at the first failure and shows the error. A provider that fails three times in a row waits behind the others for five minutes, and then one call tries it again.
fallback.range: On or off. On by default. Providers per call sets how many providers one call may try.
fallback.ex1: On: OpenAI answers with a rate limit. The call moves to your next text provider, and you get an answer.
fallback.ex2: Off: the same rate limit stops the call, and the app shows the error.
fallback.ex3: On, and a provider refuses your key: the call moves on, and that provider is skipped until you test it again or change its key.
fallback.tip: Keep it on unless you must see a failure at once, for example while you try out a new provider. Some calls never move on: a call that names its provider, speech unless Another voice is on, and embeddings, except to the same model.

fallback_attempts.title: Providers per call
fallback_attempts.short: How many providers one call may try, the first one included. A whole number from 1 to 5. The default is 3.
fallback_attempts.what: When a provider fails and the call moves on, this limits how many providers the call tries in all. The first provider counts as one. When the limit is reached, the call stops and shows the error. Each failed try takes time, so a high number can make a failing call slow. The setting does nothing while When a provider fails is off: then only one provider is tried.
fallback_attempts.range: 1 to 5, whole numbers. The default is 3. 1 means that the call does not fall back.
fallback_attempts.low: 1 or 2: a failing call stops soon. Good when an app must answer fast or not at all.
fallback_attempts.high: 4 or 5: more chances to get an answer when you have many providers. A call where all of them fail takes longer.
fallback_attempts.ex1: 1: the first provider only, as if When a provider fails were off.
fallback_attempts.ex2: 3: the first provider and two to fall back to. This is the default.
fallback_attempts.ex3: 5: you have five text providers, and a call gets an answer even when four of them are down.
fallback_attempts.tip: The number counts only the providers in your routing and, when After your choices is on, your other providers. A number higher than the providers you have changes nothing.

fallback_leaves_machine.title: Leaving this machine
fallback_leaves_machine.short: Whether a fallback from a provider on this machine may send the data to a cloud service. Off by default.
fallback_leaves_machine.what: A local AI server runs on the same machine as this AIMEAT, so the data does not leave the machine. When such a provider fails, the next provider in your routing can be a cloud service, such as OpenAI. With this setting off, that provider is skipped, and the data stays on the machine. With it on, the call moves to the cloud service, and the question and any files go there. The setting matters only when the first provider is local.
fallback_leaves_machine.range: On or off. Off by default.
fallback_leaves_machine.ex1: Off: LM Studio on this machine does not answer. The cloud provider after it is skipped, and the call shows the error.
fallback_leaves_machine.ex2: On: the same failure moves the call to OpenRouter, and the answer comes from there.
fallback_leaves_machine.ex3: Off, with OpenAI first: the setting does nothing, because the data leaves the machine in any case.
fallback_leaves_machine.tip: Keep it off when you use a local provider because the data must not leave the machine, for example personal data or confidential material. Turn it on when getting an answer matters more than where the answer is made. On a public AIMEAT, such as aimeat.io, this machine is the server, not your own computer.

fallback_pool.title: After your choices
fallback_pool.short: Whether a call may try your other providers after the ones you chose for that work, and in which order. On by default.
fallback_pool.what: In the routing you choose up to three providers for each kind of work. With this on, the call then tries your other providers that have a model set for that work. With it off, only your choices are tried. Providers per call still limits how many are tried in all. When neither your choices nor your other providers give a provider, this AIMEAT's own default answers.
fallback_pool.range: On or off, on by default. The order: in the order they are listed (the default), cheapest first, or fastest first. Cheapest first uses the text price of the model catalogue and applies to text, reading images and reading files; a provider without a price comes last. Fastest first keeps the listed order for now, because this AIMEAT does not measure speed yet.
fallback_pool.ex1: On, in the order they are listed: you chose OpenAI for text. When it fails, your Mistral and OpenRouter providers are tried next, in the order the page shows them.
fallback_pool.ex2: On, cheapest first: the cheapest of your other text providers is tried first.
fallback_pool.ex3: Off: you chose only OpenAI for text. When it fails, the call stops, even if you have other providers.
fallback_pool.tip: Keep it on, so that a call has somewhere to go. Turn it off when only the providers you chose may see the data. A provider joins this group only when you set a model for that work on it.

only_tested.title: Only tested providers
only_tested.short: Whether this AIMEAT skips your providers that have not been tested yet. On by default.
only_tested.what: When this AIMEAT picks a provider for a call, it skips your providers whose capability for that work has never been tested. This includes the providers you chose in the routing. A test is the Test now button on a provider, and a call that names the provider and works also counts. The rule does not apply when a call names its provider or its model, or runs as a role: then that choice is tried. This AIMEAT's own providers are not checked, because the people who run it answer for them. A provider that was tested but now fails is handled separately: it waits behind the providers that work.
only_tested.range: On or off. On by default.
only_tested.ex1: On: you add a Mistral provider and set a model, but you do not test it. Text calls skip it, and the page says that it has not been tested, with a Test now button.
only_tested.ex2: On, and the test works: the provider answers calls like the others.
only_tested.ex3: Off: a new provider answers calls at once. A wrong key then shows as a failed call, not as a skipped provider.
only_tested.tip: Keep it on, so that a new provider with a typing error in its key or model does not break your calls. Test each new provider once.

embeddings.title: Embeddings
embeddings.short: Turns text into numbers, so that a search finds texts that mean the same thing, not only texts with the same words. Apps and agents ask for it.
embeddings.what: An embedding is a list of numbers that a model makes from a text. Texts with a similar meaning get similar numbers, so a search by meaning can compare them. Apps and agents use embeddings to find related notes, documents or answers. Only the numbers of one model can be compared with each other. For that reason, an embedding call falls back only to the same model on another provider, never to a different model.
embeddings.range: On or off for each provider, with one model. OpenRouter, OpenAI, Mistral, a local AI server, an OpenAI-compatible address and an extension can make embeddings; Anthropic and xAI cannot. One call takes at most 256 texts and 500,000 characters.
embeddings.ex1: You search for “holiday”, and a notes app also finds the note about a trip to Crete.
embeddings.ex2: You change the embedding model: the numbers that an app stored earlier no longer match the new ones, so the app must make them again.
embeddings.tip: Choose the embedding model once and keep it. A change makes every stored embedding useless next to new ones until they are made again. In the admin settings, the default embedding model is the one that the server's own key uses. An empty field there means that the server's key makes no embeddings.

model_policy.title: Models allowed
model_policy.short: Which models your AI calls may use: any model, the recommended models, or your own list.
model_policy.what: The model policy sets which models may answer. Any model sets no limit. The recommended models are the list that the people who run this AIMEAT keep, and your policy follows their changes. With your own list, you name the models yourself. A call for a model outside the policy is refused, and the answer says which models are allowed. A call that names no model uses the provider's model when it is allowed, and otherwise the first allowed model. Whose calls says what the policy covers: your own calls, the chat, your agents and your apps.
model_policy.range: Any model (the default), the recommended models, or my own list. You can choose the recommended models only when this AIMEAT has some. Your own list takes at least 1 and at most 200 models, one per line, as type:model id. When you turn a policy on, it covers all four kinds of calls until you clear some of them.
model_policy.low: Any model: no call is refused because of its model. An app may still name its own shorter list.
model_policy.high: My own list: only the models you named answer. Every other model is refused, also in a fallback.
model_policy.ex1: Any model: an app asks for a model that you have never used, and the model answers.
model_policy.ex2: The recommended models, for my apps only: your apps use only the list that the people who run this AIMEAT keep, and your own chat may use any model.
model_policy.ex3: My own list with openai:gpt-5-mini: an agent asks for a more expensive model, and the call is refused. The answer names the allowed model.
model_policy.tip: Each layer can only make the rule stricter: both an app's own list and your list must allow a model. When you use your own list, write the models for every capability you use, also embeddings and speech. Otherwise those calls are refused.

content_classifier.title: Content Classifier
content_classifier.short: The model that gives your content a classification, such as public, internal or confidential: the decision model or a text model.
content_classifier.what: A classification decides which people and which AI may read a piece of content, and whether it may leave an organism. Rules that recognise passwords and identity codes run first. Then the Content Classifier judges the rest. A decision model answers closed questions and writes no text. A text model reads the content and answers like any text call, through your text routing or through the provider you name. The classification policy sets whether a person confirms the result and how many calls a day the classifier may make.
content_classifier.range: Decision model: the default, or a named decision provider. Text model: the text routing, or a named text provider. The operator chooses the default for this server; you may choose another one for your own content.
content_classifier.low: Answers closed questions with a probability and writes no text. The operator must turn it on for this server.
content_classifier.high: Uses your text providers and their prices. It works also when the decision model is off.
content_classifier.ex1: Decision model: default. The decision provider that this AIMEAT uses by default classifies your content. Your text routing does not change.
content_classifier.ex2: Text model: the text routing. The provider that answers your text calls also classifies your content, and the calls count toward your daily budget.
content_classifier.ex3: Text model: a named provider, such as your local AI server. Your content is classified, and the text does not go to a cloud service.
content_classifier.tip: Choose the text model when the decision model is off on this AIMEAT; the page then shows the classifier as off. Choose a local provider when your content must not leave this machine. The rules for passwords and identity codes run whichever model you choose.

daily_budget.title: Daily budget
daily_budget.short: The most your AI calls may cost in one day, in US dollars. When it is spent, further calls are refused until midnight UTC.
daily_budget.what: The budget counts what all AI calls in your name cost today: your own, your agents' and your apps', whether your own key or the server's key pays. Before each call, this AIMEAT compares what is already spent with the budget. When the amount spent reaches the budget, the call is refused, and the asker is told why. One call can go a little over the budget, because the check comes before the call and the call's own cost is known only after it. The budget starts again at midnight UTC.
daily_budget.range: 0 to 1,000 US dollars. The default is 1 dollar a day. 0 refuses every call.
daily_budget.low: A small budget: an app or an agent that goes wrong can spend only a little. Your own work can stop in the middle of the day.
daily_budget.high: A large budget: work does not stop, but a fault in an app can cost more before you see it.
daily_budget.ex1: 1: the default. Enough for many ordinary answers, because one usually costs a fraction of a cent.
daily_budget.ex2: 0: no AI call runs, for example while you are away and want no spending at all.
daily_budget.ex3: 20, with a limit of 2 on one app: the app stops at 2 dollars, and the rest of the budget stays for other work.
daily_budget.tip: Look at what your last 30 days cost, under the budget, and set the budget a little above a normal day. Give a new or busy app a limit of its own, so that it cannot use the whole budget.

app_daily_cap.title: Limit a day
app_daily_cap.short: The most one app may spend on AI in a day, in US dollars. Empty: the app may use the whole daily budget.
app_daily_cap.what: Every app may use your whole daily budget unless it has a limit of its own. A limit stops one app before it uses the budget that your other work needs. Before each call from the app, this AIMEAT compares what the app has spent today with its limit. When the app reaches its limit, its calls are refused until midnight UTC, and your other apps go on. The daily budget still applies: a limit above the budget does not let the app spend more.
app_daily_cap.range: 0 to 1,000 US dollars, written on the app's row. Empty: no limit of its own. 0 stops the app's AI calls.
app_daily_cap.low: A small limit: the app can try its AI features, but a fault in it costs little.
app_daily_cap.high: A large limit or an empty field: the app may use what is left of the daily budget.
app_daily_cap.ex1: Empty: a writing app that you use all day shares the whole budget.
app_daily_cap.ex2: 0.50: a new game that you are testing. A loop that calls the AI again and again stops at 50 cents.
app_daily_cap.ex3: 0: an app that you no longer trust. Its AI calls are refused, but the app still opens.
app_daily_cap.tip: Set a limit on a new app, and on any app whose 30-day cost surprises you. The table is ordered by 30-day cost, so the most expensive apps are at the top.

pdf_engine.title: PDF engine
pdf_engine.short: Who turns a PDF into text for a model that cannot read one itself. Only for the Reads files capability of an OpenRouter provider.
pdf_engine.what: Some models read a PDF themselves, and others read only text. OpenRouter can convert the PDF for such a model before the model reads it. This setting chooses the converter. This AIMEAT converts nothing itself. With no PDF engine or the model's own, a model that cannot read files is refused for a call with a file, and the call moves to the next provider. With Mistral OCR or Cloudflare AI, OpenRouter converts the PDF, and the model gets the text.
pdf_engine.range: No PDF engine (the default), the model's own, Mistral OCR, Cloudflare AI. The model catalogue says which models read files; a model that the catalogue does not know is trusted to read them.
pdf_engine.ex1: The model's own: your model reads PDFs itself. The PDF goes to it as it is.
pdf_engine.ex2: Mistral OCR: a scanned contract whose pages are pictures. OCR finds the text on them, and a model that reads only text can then read it.
pdf_engine.ex3: No PDF engine, with a model that reads only text: a call with a PDF skips this provider and moves to the next one that can read files.
pdf_engine.tip: Choose the model's own when your model reads files. Choose an engine when you use a model on OpenRouter that reads only text and you want it to read PDFs. For scanned pages, choose Mistral OCR.

local_only.title: This machine
local_only.short: Whether this role may use only providers on the same machine as this AIMEAT. The data then does not leave the machine.
local_only.what: With this on, the role's calls skip every provider that would take the data off this machine: OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, xAI, an address you gave, and extensions. Only a local AI server, such as LM Studio or Ollama, may answer. If the role has no such provider, its calls are refused and say why. An app can ask the same for its own role, and then the rule holds even when you leave this off.
local_only.range: On or off. Off by default.
local_only.ex1: On: a role “Diary summaries” with Ollama on this machine. The text of your diary never goes to a cloud service.
local_only.ex2: On, with only OpenAI in the role: every call of the role is refused, because no provider is on this machine.
local_only.ex3: Off: the role uses the providers you listed, wherever they run.
local_only.tip: Turn it on for a role that handles personal data or confidential content. On a public AIMEAT, such as aimeat.io, this machine is the server, and you cannot add a local provider there. The setting then works only with a local AI server that the people who run that AIMEAT offer, or on an AIMEAT you run yourself.

max_retries.title: Max retries
max_retries.short: How many times your AIMEAT asks the model again when its answer comes back empty. 1 to 10.
max_retries.what: Sometimes a model answers with nothing. A reasoning model does it most often, when its thinking uses the whole longest-answer limit. With automatic retry on, your AIMEAT asks the same question again, up to this many times. When every attempt is empty, the call fails and says why. Each new attempt is a new call, and the model can charge for it.
max_retries.range: 1 to 10. The field starts at 2. With automatic retry off, an empty answer fails at once.
max_retries.low: 1: a fault shows soon, and an empty answer costs at most one extra call.
max_retries.high: 10: a model that sometimes answers empty gets many chances. When the fault is in the settings, all ten attempts fail and cost.
max_retries.ex1: 2: the starting value. Enough for a short fault at the provider.
max_retries.ex2: 1: you test new settings and want to see an empty answer at once.
max_retries.tip: When answers often come back empty, raise the longest-answer limit or turn thinking down. More retries only repeat the same fault.

bands.title: Bands
bands.short: Two numbers from 0 to 1 that turn the rule's result into an outcome: act, ask a person, or stop.
bands.what: Each run of the rule gives a result: how sure the model is, from 0 to 1. The result is the weakest certainty among the questions that have a threshold. At or over the first number, the caller acts on its own. Under the first number but at or over the second, a person is asked. Under the second number, the caller stops. An answer under its own question's threshold stops the action before the bands are used.
bands.range: Two numbers from 0 to 1, decimals allowed. The second number must not be higher than the first. No number is filled in for you. When the model gives no certainty at all, a person is asked.
bands.low: The caller acts on its own more often, and a person sees fewer cases.
bands.high: The caller acts on its own only when the model is very sure. More cases go to a person or stop.
bands.ex1: Act 0.9, ask 0.6: with a result of 0.95 the caller acts, with 0.75 a person is asked, and with 0.4 the caller stops.
bands.ex2: Act 0.8, ask 0.8: nobody is asked. The caller acts at 0.8 or over and stops under it.
bands.ex3: Act 0.9, ask 0: the bands never stop the caller. Only an answer under its threshold stops it, and every result under 0.9 goes to a person.
bands.tip: Choose the numbers from your own examples. Try the rule on samples, read the latest decisions, and see where the right and the wrong answers fall. Start with a wide gap between the two numbers, so that a person sees the unclear cases. Make the gap narrower when the decisions show that the model is right. Fill in both numbers before you save the rule.

question_threshold.title: Threshold
question_threshold.short: The value one answer must reach, or the action stops. For a scale it is a level counted from 0. For the other question types it is a number from 0 to 1.
question_threshold.what: Only a question with a threshold counts toward the outcome. A question without one is asked and recorded, but it does not change the outcome. What the number means depends on the question type. For yes or no, it is the lowest probability of yes. For pick one, it is how sure the model must be of its pick. For a scale, it is the lowest level the answer must reach. An answer under its threshold stops the action, whatever the bands say.
question_threshold.range: Yes or no: 0 to 1. Pick one: 0 to 1. Scale: a level from 0, where 0 is the first level in your list and the highest allowed value is the last level. An empty field means the question does not count. A rule needs at least one question with a threshold.
question_threshold.low: The question stops the action only when the answer is clearly against it.
question_threshold.high: The answer must be clear, or the action stops. The action stops more often.
question_threshold.ex1: Yes or no, 0.8: the statement is 'The reply answers the customer's question'. The model must give it at least 0.8, or the reply does not go out.
question_threshold.ex2: Pick one, 0.7: a message is sorted into sales, support or billing. The model must be at least 0.7 sure of its pick, or the action stops.
question_threshold.ex3: Scale, 2: the levels are poor, fair, good and excellent (0 to 3). The answer must be good or excellent.
question_threshold.tip: Write every question so that a high value means go ahead. Then a threshold always works as a floor. Give a threshold only to the questions that must be able to stop the action. Tune the numbers from the latest decisions, not from a guess.

gate.title: Gate
gate.short: Whether an agent must wait for you when the decision model is not sure enough. Off until you turn it on.
gate.what: A gate is a decision rule that guards an action that cannot be undone, such as sending a reply. With the gate on, the agent acts only when the outcome is Act. When the outcome is Ask a person or Stop, AIMEAT tells the agent not to act, gives you a task and sends you a notification. With the gate off, the agent may act whatever the outcome is, and the decision is still recorded. A gate holds only agents. An app reads the outcome, and its own code decides.
gate.range: In the rule editor: ticked or not ticked, not ticked by default. On the agent's page: As each rule says, On for every rule, or Off. The default is As each rule says, and then the tick of each rule decides.
gate.low: Off: the agent acts on its own. You see afterwards what the model answered, and you can compare.
gate.high: On: the agent waits for you every time the model is not sure enough. This is safer, but you get more tasks.
gate.ex1: On: an agent sends replies to customers. A reply that the model is not sure of waits for you as a task.
gate.ex2: Off: the first weeks of a new rule. The agent acts, and the recorded decisions show how often the gate would have stopped it.
gate.ex3: As each rule says: the rule that guards deleting a record is ticked as a gate, and the rule that sorts messages is not.
gate.tip: Keep the gate off at first and read the decisions, so that you can compare how the agent does without it. Turn it on when a wrong action costs more than a short wait. AIMEAT does not do the action itself: it tells the agent not to act, and it records that instruction.

price_per_mtok.title: Price in USD per million tokens
price_per_mtok.short: What this provider charges for the text it reads, in US dollars per million tokens. AIMEAT uses it to count what your decisions cost.
price_per_mtok.what: Models count text in tokens, which are pieces of words. A decision provider that is an online service charges for the tokens it reads. AIMEAT computes the cost of each decision from its tokens and this price, and records the cost with the decision. The cost counts toward your daily budget and toward an agent's daily cap. The price does not change what the provider bills you. Only an online service has a price: a local decision model costs nothing.
price_per_mtok.range: 0 to 1,000 US dollars per million tokens, decimals allowed. An empty field records no price: the provider shows 'no price given', and its decisions count as free.
price_per_mtok.ex1: 0.042: the price AIMEAT uses for TypeSafe's Jev, unless the operator changes it. A decision of about 4,000 characters then costs about 0.000042 USD.
price_per_mtok.ex2: 2: a provider that charges 2 US dollars per million tokens. A decision of 1,000 tokens costs 0.002 USD.
price_per_mtok.ex3: Empty: you do not know the price yet. The decisions are recorded at no cost, so your daily budget does not limit them.
price_per_mtok.tip: Copy the price from the provider's price list: the price for the text it reads (input). Leave the field empty only while you do not know the price. Without a price, your daily budget and an agent's daily cap do not count these decisions.

provider_limits.title: What it can carry
provider_limits.short: The most options this provider chooses among, and the most text it reads, in characters. AIMEAT refuses a question that does not fit, before anything is sent.
provider_limits.what: Each decision model has limits. Some models read only the start of a long text and drop the rest without an error. Then the decision rests on part of the content. Here you tell AIMEAT the limits of this provider. AIMEAT checks every request against them before it sends anything. It also refuses a rule that names this provider when the rule's questions do not fit. The text that counts is the content and the questions together.
provider_limits.range: Most options: a whole number from 2 to 10,000. An empty field means 20. Most text: 256 to 4,000,000 characters. AIMEAT counts about 4 characters as one token. An empty field means about 4,000 characters (4,096). These are the least a local model carries.
provider_limits.low: AIMEAT refuses more questions, but no content is cut off without a word.
provider_limits.high: Longer content and more options get through. If a limit is higher than the model really carries, the model can answer from part of the content.
provider_limits.ex1: 20 and 4,096: the built-in local example Laya. It reads about 4,000 characters, so AIMEAT refuses a longer message before it sends it.
provider_limits.ex2: 60 and 20,000: the built-in local example jeff, which chose well among 60 topics when it was measured. A pick-one question with 61 options is refused.
provider_limits.tip: Take the numbers from the provider's documentation, or measure them: put a known fact at the end of a long text and see whether the answer uses it. When a question is refused, send fewer fields, or split a long list of options into parts.

store_state.title: Keep the cleaned text with each decision
store_state.short: When on, each decision keeps the text the model judged, after personal data was removed. When off, only a fingerprint of the text is kept. Off by default.
store_state.what: AIMEAT removes personal data before it sends content to the decision model. This setting decides what the decision record keeps of that cleaned text. When on, the record keeps the whole text, so you can see later exactly what the model judged. When off, the record keeps only a fingerprint: a short code computed from the text. The fingerprint shows whether two decisions were about the same content, but the text cannot be read back from it. A decision record is deleted after a year, unless the operator set another period.
store_state.range: Off by default. The setting applies to the decisions made after you change it.
store_state.tip: Turn it on while you tune a rule, so that you can see what the model judged. Turn it off when the decisions go well, so that less of your content is kept. Content that an app or agent sent as public, without removing personal data, is kept as it was sent.

public_opt_out.title: Let my apps and agents send content they mark as public without removing personal data
public_opt_out.short: When on, an app or agent may send content it marks as public without removing personal data. Off by default.
public_opt_out.what: By default, AIMEAT removes personal data from everything that goes to the decision model: e-mail addresses, phone numbers, Finnish identity codes, bank account numbers, street addresses and names. An app or agent can mark content as public, for example a published news article with nothing private in it. With this setting on, AIMEAT sends such content as it is. With this setting off, AIMEAT removes personal data from all content, whatever the app or agent says about it.
public_opt_out.range: Off by default. Content that you mark as public yourself is always sent as it is.
public_opt_out.tip: Turn it on only if you trust every app and agent that asks the decision model for you. An app can mark anything as public, and AIMEAT does not check the mark. With an online service, the content then leaves this machine with any personal data in it. TypeSafe runs in the United States and may keep what it receives.

daily_cap.title: Daily cap
daily_cap.short: The most this agent may spend on AI in one day, in US dollars. An empty field means no cap of its own.
daily_cap.what: Every AI call the agent makes costs money: its decisions and the text it writes. This cap counts both together. Before each call, your AIMEAT compares what the agent spent today with the cap. When the agent has reached the cap, your AIMEAT refuses its next calls until the day changes. One call can go a little over the cap, because its cost is known only after the call. Your own daily budget still applies.
daily_cap.range: 0 to 10,000 US dollars. Empty: no cap of its own, and only your daily budget limits the agent. 0 stops every AI call of this agent. The day changes at midnight UTC.
daily_cap.low: A low cap protects you when the agent goes wrong, for example in a loop. On a busy day the agent stops, and its work waits until the next day.
daily_cap.high: A high cap lets the agent finish long work on the same day. A fault, such as a loop, costs more before the agent stops.
daily_cap.ex1: 0: you want the agent to stop using AI for now. Every call is refused at once.
daily_cap.ex2: 0.5: an agent that makes short decisions, such as sorting messages. A loop stops at 50 cents.
daily_cap.ex3: 5: an agent that writes long reports with a large model. It finishes a day's work, and a fault costs at most about 5 dollars.
daily_cap.tip: Set a cap for every agent that works while nobody watches it. Look at the figure for today under the cap for a few days, and set the cap a little above a normal day. When the agent stops in the middle of the day, check the cap first.

run_mode.title: How it runs
run_mode.short: Whether your connector starts this agent only when work arrives, or keeps it running all the time.
run_mode.what: An agent of your own is a program that runs on a machine. Your connector is the program on that machine that starts your agents. This setting tells your connector when to start this agent. Your AIMEAT stores the choice and shows it, and your connector acts on it. When no connector runs the agent, the setting changes nothing.
run_mode.range: Starts when work arrives, Always on, Not decided. A new agent made on this page starts with Starts when work arrives. An agent made another way starts as Not decided.
run_mode.low: Nothing of the agent runs while it waits. The first answer comes a few seconds later, because the program must start first. Good for work that comes now and then: reports, sorting, research.
run_mode.high: The agent answers at once, but its program runs on the machine all the time. Good for a front door that people talk to, where a wait of a few seconds is felt.
run_mode.ex1: Starts when work arrives: an agent that writes a news summary every morning. It runs for a few minutes a day.
run_mode.ex2: Always on: a customer service agent on your website. A visitor gets an answer without a wait.
run_mode.ex3: Not decided: an agent that you still test by hand. Your connector does not start it.
run_mode.tip: Pick Starts when work arrives unless a person waits for the answer. You can change between all three at any time. When an agent does not answer at all, check this setting first: Not decided means that your connector does not start it.

concurrency.title: Max concurrent tasks
concurrency.short: How many tasks the agent works on at the same time. 1 to 20; 1 means one task after another.
concurrency.what: Tasks wait in the agent's queue. With 1, the agent finishes one task before it starts the next. With a higher number, it starts several tasks at once, so a long queue empties sooner. Your AIMEAT stores the number, and the program that runs the agent keeps to it. A number above 1 needs a program that can do several tasks at once, such as the CrewAI daemon of the aimeat-crewai package.
concurrency.low: 1: one task at a time. It works with every program that runs agents.
concurrency.high: More than 1: a long queue empties sooner. The tasks use the same machine and the same daily cap, and a task can finish before one that came earlier.
concurrency.ex1: 1: an agent that writes into the same document in every task. Two tasks at once could write over each other.
concurrency.ex2: 3: an agent that answers separate customer questions. Three people get an answer at the same time.
concurrency.ex3: 10: an agent that checks a hundred web pages, one page in each task.
concurrency.tip: Keep 1 unless the queue grows faster than the agent empties it. Raise the number only when the tasks do not depend on each other. First make sure that the program that runs the agent can do several tasks at once.

self_start.title: Starts work by itself
self_start.short: On: work sent to the agent starts at once. Off: the work waits until you start it.
self_start.what: Work reaches an agent as tasks: from you, from a schedule or from another agent. With this switch on, the agent starts each task at once, and you see afterwards what it did. With the switch off, each task waits in the queue until you press Start, or ask your AI to start it. An agent that can spend money, send mail or delete things in your name always waits for your OK, and the switch does not turn on. The agent cannot change this setting for itself.
self_start.range: On or off. When nobody has set it, an agent made to run tasks starts by itself, and every other agent waits.
self_start.ex1: On: an agent that writes a news summary every morning from a schedule. Nobody needs to be awake to start it.
self_start.ex2: Off: a new agent that you do not know well yet. You read its plan and press Start.
self_start.ex3: Always off: an agent that may pay invoices. Every payment waits for your OK, and the switch does not turn on.
self_start.tip: Start with off, and turn the switch on when the agent has done the same kind of work well a few times. A task can carry its own word, such as "check with me first", and that word goes before this switch.

purchase_limit.title: Most it may spend in a day
purchase_limit.short: How much money this agent may spend on purchases in one day, in the currency you pick. Without a limit, it spends nothing.
purchase_limit.what: An agent can buy things in your name, and the money comes from you. This limit sets how much it may spend in one day. Before each purchase, your AIMEAT adds the price to what the agent spent today. When the sum would go over the limit, the purchase is refused, and the agent is told where you can raise the limit. Each currency has its own limit. In a currency with no limit, the agent cannot spend money at all.
purchase_limit.range: 0 to 1,000,000, in euros or US dollars. When you remove the limit, the agent spends nothing in that currency. The day changes at midnight UTC. A hold for a bid counts as spent, also when the hold is released later the same day.
purchase_limit.low: A low limit keeps a mistake small. The agent stops at the first purchase that does not fit.
purchase_limit.high: A high limit lets the agent make larger purchases by itself. A wrong purchase can cost up to the limit.
purchase_limit.ex1: 20 EUR: an agent that buys single reports or data sets. A wrong purchase costs at most 20 euros a day.
purchase_limit.ex2: 50 EUR and no limit in USD: the agent can pay in euros, and a purchase priced in dollars is refused.
purchase_limit.ex3: 500 EUR: an agent that orders supplies for your company. Each day's orders stay under 500 euros.
purchase_limit.tip: Set the lowest limit that lets the agent do its job, and check on the card what it spent today. The limit does not apply to your own purchases or to morsel prices. Only you can change the limit, signed in yourself.

scopes.title: What it may do
scopes.short: Which permissions the agent gets. Each permission lets it read or change one kind of thing in your name. You can narrow them later.
scopes.what: A permission lets the agent read or change one kind of thing, for example read your memory or write to it. The agent can do only what its permissions allow. When it tries something else, your AIMEAT refuses and names the permission that is missing. The fewer permissions an agent has, the less harm a mistake or a stolen key can do. An agent that can spend money, send mail or delete things in your name never starts a task by itself.
scopes.range: A new agent: Reading only, Read and write, Everything you can do. A token: Only these (you pick each permission), Everything you can, and for the operator of this server, Run the whole server.
scopes.low: Reading only: the agent reads your memory, your files, the public directory and the boards you can reach, and changes nothing. Read and write also lets it write to your memory and files, ask other agents to do work for you, and see the work in your queue.
scopes.high: Everything you can do: the agent can do all that you can, in every app and with every piece of data. A mistake or a stolen key reaches everything. After some days your AIMEAT knows which permissions the agent used. From then on, its tasks wait for your OK, and your AIMEAT offers to narrow its permissions to those.
scopes.ex1: Reading only: an agent that answers questions about your notes in a chat. It cannot change or delete anything.
scopes.ex2: Read and write: an agent that collects news and saves a summary in your memory.
scopes.ex3: Only these, with memory writing only: a measuring device that saves its readings. If its token leaks, nobody can read your data with it.
scopes.tip: Give the least that the job needs, and add a permission when the agent is refused. Use Everything you can do only for your own AI, which you trust as you trust yourself.

process.title: Process
process.short: Sequential: the tasks run one after another in the order of the list. Hierarchical: a manager gives the tasks to the members and checks their work.
process.what: A crew is a group of members, and each task names the member that does it. With Sequential, the crew runs the tasks in the order of the list, and a task can read the results of earlier tasks. With Hierarchical, the crew adds a manager that plans the work, gives each task to the member it thinks fits, and checks the answer before it goes on. The manager is also a model, so a run makes more model calls and costs more.
process.range: Sequential or Hierarchical. The default is Sequential.
